Before you start

How this course works

Build Pip's Peak, a platformer with four levels, enemies, power-ups, music and a boss, in TIC-80.

Pip's Peak is a small platformer. Pip, a sprout with a leaf on its head, runs and jumps through a meadow, a crystal cave and a sky tower, collecting coins and gems, stomping slimes and dodging bats and turrets, until it reaches the throne room of King Glob.

What you need

  • TIC-80 1.3.1, a free fantasy computer, from tic80.com. It is a whole studio in one program: a code editor, a sprite editor, a map editor, a sound editor and a music tracker. It runs on Windows, macOS, Linux and in a web browser.
  • A keyboard. TIC-80's buttons are the arrow keys and Z X A S; in this course Z is the jump button (button "A").
  • No experience. The game is written in Lua, and each new idea is explained the first time it appears.

How a lesson works

  • The line above each panel says where the code goes: a new function (add it), a function that replaces your old version of it, or lines in a function, after a line you already have. Lines that are new in this lesson have a green bar on the left.
  • Each lesson's new and changed definitions (constants, tables, variables: everything outside the functions) are collected in one panel. Constants go at the top of the cart, tables like SPAWN after the functions they name, as the panel says.
  • Optional Challenges at the end of each lesson push you to go further! Are you up for it?
  • At the bottom of every lesson you can open the whole cart's code after that lesson, and every change since the lesson before, so you can always compare your code with the course's.

If you fall behind or something breaks, load the lesson's finished cart from the top of the lesson and carry on from there: see Loading a lesson cart. The Helpful tips in the lesson list cover loading and saving carts, the keys and the console, and fixing errors.

Lesson 1 of 20 · 30 minutes

Meet TIC-80

Find your way around the TIC-80 studio and write your first program, a ball you move with the arrow keys.

In this lesson

  • what a fantasy computer is
  • the console and its commands
  • the code editor
  • the game loop, TIC()
  • drawing with cls, rect, circ and print
  • reading buttons with btn

Starting point: an empty cart · Finished: lesson01.png · Play it

Step 1 Start TIC-80

Download TIC-80 1.3.1 from tic80.com and start it (or open it in your browser). After a short intro you land in the console: a black screen with a prompt.

TIC-80 is a fantasy computer: a pretend games machine with tight, fixed limits. The screen is 240 x 136 pixels, there are 16 colors on screen at once, 4 sound channels, and every game fits in one cart file.

Type help commands and press Enter to see the list of commands. The ones you need:

CommandDoes
new luaStart a new cart that uses Lua (it comes with a small demo)
save pips-peakSave the cart
load pips-peakLoad a cart
runRun the game (CtrlR does the same from anywhere)
dir, cdList the files in the current folder, change folder
folderOpen the folder TIC-80 keeps your carts in

Type new lua.

Run the demo before you change anything: press CtrlR. The demo says "HELLO WORLD!", and the arrow keys move its little sprite. Press Esc to come back.

Step 2 Open the code editor

Press F1 (or click the first tab at the top left). This is the code editor. Select all of the demo with CtrlA and delete it.

Step 3 Write the game loop

Type this program in (or copy it and paste it with CtrlV):

The first four lines are comments (Lua ignores everything after -- on a line), but TIC-80 reads them: they give the cart its title, author, description and language.

Then come three variables: x and y, the ball's position, and t, a frame counter. They are written outside any function and without the word local, which makes them globals: they keep their values from one frame to the next.

TIC() is the heart of every TIC-80 game. TIC-80 calls TIC() 60 times every second. Each call is one frame, and in each frame the game does the same three things:

  1. Read the buttons and change the variables: btn(3) is true while the right arrow is held, so x grows by one pixel every frame.
  2. Clear the screen, so the last frame's picture disappears.
  3. Draw everything again where it is now.

This is the game loop.

Two pieces of Lua in it are new:

  • if btn(3) then x = x + 1 end runs the part between then and end only when the condition is true. An if always needs its end; it can also span several lines.
  • "frame " .. t joins two pieces of text: .. turns the number t into text and puts it after "frame ".

Step 4 Run it

Press CtrlR. Move the ball with the arrow keys. Press Esc to stop the game and come back to the editor.

Check your work

You see a sky-blue screen with green grass at the bottom, "HELLO, TIC-80!" near the top and a frame counter in the corner counting up. The yellow ball moves one pixel per frame while you hold an arrow key, and it can leave the screen.

If TIC-80 shows an error instead, read it: it says the line number. The usual causes are a missing end, or a typo in a function name (Lua cares about capital letters: Cls is not cls).

Step 5 Understand the drawing functions

The screen is a grid of 240 x 136 pixels. (0, 0) is the top-left corner; x grows to the right and y grows down. So the grass at y = 112 is near the bottom.

FunctionDraws
cls(color)Fills the whole screen with one color
rect(x, y, w, h, color)A filled rectangle, top-left corner at x, y
circ(x, y, r, color)A filled circle, center at x, y, radius r (center to edge)
print(text, x, y, color)Text

Colors are numbers from 0 to 15. TIC-80 starts with this palette (lesson 4 shows how to change it):

Buttons are numbers too: btn(0) up, btn(1) down, btn(2) left, btn(3) right, btn(4) is button A (Z), btn(5) is B (X). TIC-80 has no names for them, so btn(RIGHT) does not work.

The API reference lists every TIC-80 function with examples.

Step 6 Save your cart

Press Esc until you see the console and type save pips-peak. From now on CtrlS saves it under that name.

Challenge Keep the ball on the screen

The ball can disappear off the edges. Make it stop at the edges instead.

Hint

After moving, check x: if it is less than 6 (the radius), set it back to 6. Do the same at the right edge (240 - 6), the top (6) and the bottom; the bottom can be the top of the grass (112 - 6), so the ball rolls on it.

One way to do it

math.min picks the smaller number and math.max the larger, so together they clamp x between 6 and 234.

See what it might look like

After moving, the ball's x and y are clamped, so it stops at the screen's edges and on top of the grass. Hold an arrow key until it reaches an edge.

Challenge A ball that changes color

While Z is held, draw the ball in a different color.

Hint

btn(4) is button A, the Z key. Choose the color in a variable before calling circ.

See what it might look like

The color is chosen in a variable before circ: yellow, or red while Z is held. Move the ball and hold Z.

Challenge A sunny sky

Draw a sun with circ, and a cloud made of three overlapping white circles. Draw them after cls and before the ball, so the ball passes in front of them.

See what it might look like

A sun and a cloud of three white circles, drawn right after the sky and the grass, so the ball moves in front of the cloud.

Lesson 2 of 20 · 40 minutes

Drawing Pip in the sprite editor

Draw the game's hero pixel by pixel in TIC-80's sprite editor, then put it on the screen with spr().

In this lesson

  • the sprite editor and its tools
  • TILES and SPRITES, and sprite numbers
  • drawing a sprite with the palette
  • the transparent color
  • spr()
  • tables and constants in Lua

Starting point: lesson01.png · Finished: lesson02.png · Play it

Step 1 Open the sprite editor

Press F2. The sprite editor has three parts: the sprite you are drawing (the big canvas), the colors you draw with (the palette) and every sprite in the cart (the sheet on the right).

A sprite is a small picture, 8 x 8 pixels. The sheet holds 512 of them in two tabs:

  • TILES, numbers 0-255: pictures the map can be built from (ground, walls; lesson 6).
  • SPRITES, numbers 256-511: everything else, like characters, enemies and items.

The number of the selected sprite is shown above the canvas. You draw a sprite on the screen by its number, so it matters where you put it.

Step 2 Pick Pip's slot

Click the SPRITES tab (the second small tab left of the sheet), then click the top-left square of the sheet. The canvas shows #256: the first sprite on the SPRITES tab. Pip lives here.

Step 3 Draw Pip

Pip is a little green sprout with a leaf on its head, a yellow face and orange feet. Here is the sprite, zoomed in with a grid, and the same picture as rows of digits: each digit is one pixel's color number, and 0 means leave it empty.

To draw it:

  1. Click a color in the palette (it gets a white frame). Pip uses 5 lime for the leaf, 6 green, 4 yellow for the face, 15 slate for the eye (written f in the rows) and 3 orange for the feet.
  2. Make sure the brush tool is selected (the first tool under the canvas).
  3. Click the canvas to set pixels. Holding the button down draws while you move.

Here is the whole drawing, done in TIC-80's sprite editor the way artists often work: the outline first, in Pip's main color; the fill tool for the inside; then the face, the leaf, the feet and the eye on top. Watch the feet: one pixel lands in the wrong place, and CtrlZ takes it back.

Check your drawing: the number above the canvas says #256, and your Pip matches the rows of digits on the card, pixel for pixel.

The other tools help: the picker takes a color from the canvas, select lets you move part of the sprite, fill floods an area, and the next buttons flip, rotate or clear the sprite.

Color 0 is special. When you draw a sprite, you can tell TIC-80 to skip one color so the background shows through. This course always skips color 0, so empty pixels are see-through. Don't use color 0 inside a sprite unless you want a hole there.

Explore Pip in the Sprite Lab: the real sprite editor, with this lesson's cart. Point at any part of the editor to find out what it does, try drawing on Pip, then press ▶ Try it in the game to see your Pip on the screen (press Esc to come back).

Step 4 Put Pip on the screen

Go back to the code editor (F1) and replace the whole program with this one:

Three new ideas:

  • Constants. local BTN_LEFT, BTN_RIGHT = 2, 3 gives the button numbers names, and local PIP = 256 names the sprite. local means these names belong to this file only; we use it for values that never change. Names in capitals are a common way to say "this is a constant".
  • A table. player = {x = 116, y = 104} groups the player's numbers in one variable. You read and change them as player.x and player.y.
  • spr(id, x, y, colorkey) draws sprite id with its top-left corner at x, y. The colorkey (here 0) is the transparent color.

Pip stands at y = 104 so that its feet touch the grass: the grass starts at 112, and a sprite is 8 pixels tall.

Step 5 Run it

Press CtrlR and walk Pip left and right.

Check your work

Pip stands on the grass in the middle of the screen and moves one pixel per frame with the left and right arrows. Around Pip you see sky, not a black square: color 0 is transparent.

If Pip is a black square, the 0 at the end of spr(PIP, player.x, player.y, 0) is missing. If you see nothing, check that you drew in slot 256 (SPRITES tab, top left) and not on the TILES tab.

Challenge A bigger Pip

spr can take more numbers after the color key: spr(id, x, y, colorkey, scale). Draw Pip at scale 2 next to the normal one.

Hint

spr(PIP, 20, 96, 0, 2) draws Pip twice as big. At scale 2 it is 16 pixels tall, so it needs to start 8 pixels higher to stand on the grass.

See what it might look like

spr(PIP, 20, 96, 0, 2) draws a second Pip at scale 2, standing on the grass at the left; here the normal Pip has walked over next to it.

Challenge Pip in a hat

Select sprite 257 and draw your own version of Pip (a hat, a scarf, different colors). Change PIP to 257 to see it in the game, then change it back.

See what it might look like

Sprite 257 is Pip in a little top hat (slate with a red band) where its leaf was, and PIP is 257, so the game draws that one.

Challenge Up and down

Let Pip move up and down too, with buttons 0 and 1. Add the constants BTN_UP, BTN_DOWN = 0, 1.

See what it might look like

With BTN_UP and BTN_DOWN, the up and down arrows change player.y too, so Pip can go anywhere on the screen (nothing stops it at the grass yet). Try the four arrow keys.

Lesson 3 of 20 · 45 minutes

Animation

Draw Pip's running, jumping and falling frames, and flip through them in code so Pip walks.

In this lesson

  • animation frames
  • copying and editing sprites
  • a frame counter
  • integer division // and the remainder %
  • Lua lists
  • flipping a sprite

Starting point: lesson02.png · Finished: lesson03.png · Play it

Step 1 Draw the animation frames

An animation is a few pictures shown one after another. Pip needs seven more:

SpriteFrame
257standing, breathing out (one pixel lower)
258 - 261running: four steps
262jumping (legs spread)
263falling (leaf blown up)

You don't have to draw each frame from scratch. In the sprite editor:

  1. Select sprite 256 and press CtrlC to copy it.
  2. Click sprite 257 and press CtrlV to paste.
  3. Change the pixels that differ. The rows of digits under the picture above show every frame exactly.

Repeat for 258 to 263. Keep all frames facing right: the code flips them when Pip goes left.

When a frame moves a whole part by a pixel, you don't redraw it: pick the select tool (the third one under the canvas), drag a box round the part, and click the little arrows that appear round the canvas to nudge it.

Compare 258 and 259: in 259 the body is one pixel lower and the feet have moved. Small changes look like smooth motion at 60 frames a second.

The Sprite Lab plays the animation while you draw: click a running frame, and the lab plays ANIM_RUN the way this lesson's game does. Change a pixel in one frame and watch the animation change.

Step 2 Count the frames

Add a frame counter. It goes up by one every frame and works as the clock for all animations. Start from your lesson 2 code. Replace its constants (the single PIP constant is gone: Pip's sprites now come in lists) and add the counter:

An animation is a list: a table whose entries are numbered 1, 2, 3 … ANIM_RUN[1] is 258 and #ANIM_RUN (the length) is 4.

PIP is gone, so TIC has nothing to draw yet. In TIC, replace the spr(PIP, ...) line with these two, to try the list:

Check

Run it (CtrlR): Pip stands on the grass in its first running frame, 258, legs apart. It still walks with the arrow keys.

Step 3 Pick the frame to show

This function returns the sprite to draw now for an animation:

Step by step, for ANIM_RUN at speed 6:

  • t // speed is integer division: it counts up by one every 6 frames (0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, …).
  • % #frames is the remainder after dividing by 4, so it goes 0, 1, 2, 3, 0, 1, 2, 3, …
  • + 1 because Lua lists start at 1.

So the frame changes every 6 frames, and loops: 258, 259, 260, 261, 258, …

Try it in TIC: make t = t + 1 its first line, so the clock ticks, and change the first of your two new lines to:

Check

Run it: Pip runs on the spot all the time, even when you press nothing. Those are your frames 258 to 261, one after another.

Step 4 Update and draw in separate functions

The game loop is growing, so split it: update_player changes the state, draw_player only draws.

p is the player table passed in (update_player(player)), so p.x is player.x. Moving left sets p.flip = 1, moving right sets it to 0, and p.moving remembers whether Pip moved this frame.

spr's sixth argument flips the sprite: 0 as drawn, 1 mirrored left to right. Running uses a fast animation (a new frame every 6 frames); standing a slow one (every 30 frames, like breathing).

Check

Run it: nothing changes yet (Pip still runs on the spot), but there's no error. Nothing calls the two new functions until the new TIC.

Now replace your whole TIC, test lines and all, with this one:

Step 5 Run it

Press CtrlR and walk left and right.

Check your work

Standing still, Pip breathes (moves up and down one pixel every half second). Running, its feet move. Pip faces the way it's going.

Challenge Faster feet

Make the run animation faster or slower and decide what looks best. Try 3, 6 and 10: when do the feet look like they're slipping on the ground, and when do they look like they're running in slow motion?

Challenge Blink

Draw a frame where Pip's eye is closed in sprite 266 (copy 256 there and change the eye pixel to green; 264 and 265 get used in later lessons). Make Pip blink: show that frame for 6 frames every 2 seconds while standing.

Hint

t % 120 < 6 is true for 6 frames out of every 120 (2 seconds).

See what it might look like

Sprite 266 is Pip with its eye closed (the eye pixel is green). While Pip stands still, t % 120 < 6 shows it for 6 frames every 2 seconds; running, Pip doesn't blink.

Challenge Turn around slowly

When Pip changes direction, show a "turning" frame (draw it in sprite 267) for 4 frames before running the other way.

See what it might look like

Sprite 267 is Pip facing us. Pressing the other direction starts a 4-frame turn: Pip shows that frame and waits, then runs the other way. Run left and right with the arrow keys.

+t = 0   -- frame counter: animations use it as their clock

+-- == Animation ==
+-- The sprite to show now for an animation that changes every `speed` frames.
+function anim_frame(frames, speed)
+  return
+    frames[(t // speed) % #frames + 1]
+end
+
+-- == Player ==
+function update_player(p)
+  p.moving = false
+  if btn(BTN_LEFT) then
+    p.x = p.x - 1
+    p.flip = 1          -- the sprites face right; flip them to face left
+    p.moving = true
+  end
+  if btn(BTN_RIGHT) then
+    p.x = p.x + 1
+    p.flip = 0
+    p.moving = true
+  end
+end
+
+function draw_player(p)
+  local id
+  if p.moving then
+    id = anim_frame(ANIM_RUN, 6)
+  else
+    id = anim_frame(ANIM_IDLE, 30)
+  end
+  spr(id, p.x, p.y, 0, 1, p.flip)
+end
 
 -- == Game loop ==

-  end

Lesson 4 of 20 · 35 minutes

Palettes and color

Change TIC-80's 16 colors in the palette editor, then change them from code to turn day into night.

In this lesson

  • the palette editor and RGB colors
  • how one palette color is shared by every sprite
  • hexadecimal
  • the palette in memory (peek and poke)
  • saving and restoring colors
  • BOOT()

Starting point: lesson03.png · Finished: lesson04.png · Play it

Step 1 Look at the palette

TIC-80 shows 16 colors at a time, numbered 0 to 15. Every sprite pixel, tile and shape stores a color number, not a color. The palette says which actual color each number shows. So if you change palette color 6, everything green in the game changes at once: Pip, the grass, the bushes.

So a few changed colors can make a cave darker, a sunset redder or an enemy flash, without redrawing anything.

Step 2 Edit a color in the palette editor

In the sprite editor (F2), switch on the advanced view with the small button at the top left. A new button appears to the right of the palette: click it, and the tools are replaced by three sliders.

Each color is a mix of red, green and blue, each from 0 to 255. The values are also shown in hexadecimal (base 16, digits 0-9 and A-F): B1 3E 53 means red B1 (177), green 3E (62), blue 53 (83). Programmers often write a whole color as one hex number: 0xb13e53.

Try it: select color 6 (the green), drag its sliders and watch Pip change on the canvas and the sheet. Put it back to 38 B7 64 when you're done: undo (CtrlZ) doesn't cover palette changes, so note a color's old values before you change it.

Changes you make here are saved in the cart, so the game always starts with them.

Or try it in the Sprite Lab, which opens the palette editor on color 6 (green).

Step 3 Find the palette in memory

TIC-80 has 96 KB of memory (RAM), and parts of it have fixed jobs. The palette the screen uses lives at address 0x3FC0: 16 colors x 3 bytes, red then green then blue. Color 0 is at 0x3FC0-0x3FC2, color 1 at 0x3FC3, and so on: color i starts at 0x3FC0 + i * 3.

Two functions read and write memory: peek(address) returns the byte there, poke(address, value) writes one.

New and changed definitions outside the functions (constants, tables, variables): add these to your cart, or replace the old version of the same lines.

get_color reads the three bytes of color i and packs them into one number like 0x41a6f6: << shifts the red byte 16 bits to the left, green 8 bits, and | combines them.

set_color does the opposite: rgb >> 16 & 0xff shifts the number right and keeps the lowest 8 bits, which is the red byte.

Test both functions: add this line at the very bottom of your code, below TIC's end. It copies color 2 (red) into color 10, the sky:

Check

Run it (CtrlR): the sky is red. The grass and Pip don't change: only color 10 does.

Now delete the test line. Code outside any function runs when the game starts, so if it stays, the next step saves the red sky as a day color.

Step 4 Make night fall

Add the night colors, a flag, and somewhere to keep the cart's own colors:

BOOT() is the second function TIC-80 calls on its own: once, when the game starts, before the first TIC(). Here it saves the starting palette:

Check

Run it: nothing changes yet (the sky is blue again), but there's no error. BOOT has saved all 16 colors in day_colors.

When the palette changes, put all 16 day colors back first, then apply the night ones on top:

pairs(NIGHT) goes through every entry of the table: i is the color number (10, 6 or 12), rgb its new color.

Try night out first. Add these two lines at the end of BOOT, before its end:

Check

Run it: the game starts at night. The sky is dark blue, and the grass and Pip are teal: they share color 6, so both change.

Delete the two test lines again, or the game always starts at night.

Toggle night with Z: replace your TIC() with this one. btnp is like btn, but true only on the frame the button goes down, so one press toggles once instead of 60 times a second:

Check your work

Run it (CtrlR) and press Z: the sky turns dark blue, the grass teal, and the sun becomes a pale moon. Press it again and the day comes back.

Lesson 5 removes this day/night code again: Z becomes the jump button.

Challenge Sunset

Add a third look: press Z to go from day to sunset to night and back. Choose sunset colors for the sky (10) and grass (6).

Hint

Replace the true/false night with a number 0, 1, 2 and a table of looks: LOOKS = {{}, {[10] = 0xef7d57}, NIGHT}.

See what it might look like

look is now 0, 1 or 2 and picks one of three tables in LOOKS: day, sunset (an orange sky and olive grass) and night. Press Z to go round them.

Challenge Flash

Make the whole screen flash white for 4 frames when you press X (button 5), by setting every color to white and then calling apply_palette().

See what it might look like

X sets all 16 colors to white, and 4 frames later apply_palette() puts the normal (or night) colors back. Press X, and Z for night.

Challenge Read it back

Use trace(string.format("%06x", get_color(10))) to print the sky color in the console while the game runs. Check the value in the palette editor: by day they match. At night the console shows 29366f, but the editor still shows the saved color, 41a6f6: code changes the palette the game runs with, not the one saved in the cart.

Lesson 5 of 20 · 40 minutes

Gravity and jumping

Give Pip a vertical speed, pull it down with gravity, and jump with Z, higher the longer you hold it.

In this lesson

  • velocity and acceleration
  • gravity
  • jumping with btnp
  • variable jump height
  • choosing sprites for jumping and falling

Starting point: lesson04.png · Finished: lesson05.png · Play it

Step 1 Speed, not position

So far Pip's position changes by a fixed amount when you press a button. Jumping needs one more idea: velocity, how fast Pip is moving and in which direction. We store the vertical speed in vy, in pixels per frame. Negative is up (y grows downward), positive is down.

Every frame:

  1. Gravity adds a little to vy: Pip falls faster and faster.
  2. y changes by vy.
  3. If Pip went below the ground, put it back on the ground and stop it.

A jump is setting vy to a big negative number. Gravity then slows the rise, stops it, and brings Pip back down.

Step 2 Add the constants

Remove lesson 4's day/night code: get_color, set_color, apply_palette, NIGHT, night, day_colors, BOOT and PALETTE_ADDR, and in TIC the Z check, the sun/moon line and the "Z: day/night" text (Z is about to become the jump button). Keep BTN_A.

Check

Run it (CtrlR): it's lesson 3's game again: sky, grass, and Pip walking. No sun, no text, and Z does nothing. If you get an error, it names something you deleted that is still used, like BOOT still calling get_color: delete that too.

Now add these constants:

New and changed definitions outside the functions (constants, tables, variables): add these to your cart, or replace the old version of the same lines.

All of these are tuning numbers: change them and the game feels different. With these values, Pip rises 30 pixels in 16 frames.

Frame123…1516
vy-3.75-3.5-3.25…-0.250
height3.757.2510.5…3030

Step 3 Jump and fall

The player now has a vertical speed, knows whether it is on the ground, and whether it is in a jump:

Check

Run it: nothing changes yet, but there's no error.

Here is the new half of update_player:

  • btnp(BTN_A) and p.ground: jump only when standing, and only on the press.
  • Variable jump height: while rising from a jump, letting go of Z cuts the upward speed to -1.5, so the jump ends early. p.jumping makes sure only a jump you started can be cut short (later, springs and bounces also throw Pip up).
  • math.min(p.vy + GRAVITY, MAX_FALL) adds gravity but never lets Pip fall faster than 4 pixels per frame, so long falls stay controllable.

Check

Run it and press Z: Pip jumps and lands on the grass again. Hold Z for a high jump, tap it for a hop. In the air Pip still shows its standing or running frames.

Step 4 Show jumping and falling

In the air, Pip shows sprite 262 while going up and 263 while coming down.

Check your work

Run it: in the air, Pip now shows its jump frame going up and its fall frame coming down. Z makes Pip jump; holding it longer jumps higher. You can't jump again in mid-air. Pip runs and jumps at the same time, and lands back on the grass.

Challenge Moon gravity

Try GRAVITY = 0.1. What else do you need to change so the jump is still about 30 pixels high? (A jump rises a little less than JUMP_SPEED * JUMP_SPEED / (2 * GRAVITY) pixels, because gravity is added in whole-frame steps.) With the slower fall, does a tap still give a short hop, or does JUMP_CUT need changing too?

See what it might look like

GRAVITY = 0.1 and JUMP_SPEED = -2.5: 2.5 * 2.5 / (2 * 0.1) is about 30, so the jump is as high as before but slow and floaty. Hold Z for a full jump.

Challenge Double jump

Let Pip jump once more in mid-air. Add a field air_jumps that is set to 1 when Pip lands, and allow a jump in the air while it is above 0.

Hint

In the jump check: if btnp(BTN_A) and (p.ground or p.air_jumps > 0) then, and subtract one from air_jumps when the jump happens in the air.

See what it might look like

Pip does a normal jump, then a double jump: pressing Z again at the top takes it twice as high.

Challenge Floaty fall

While Z is held and Pip is falling, use a smaller MAX_FALL (say 1.2) so Pip glides down slowly.

See what it might look like

While Pip falls with Z held, the fall speed is capped at 1.2 instead of 4, so Pip glides down. Here Pip first lets go of Z at the top (a normal fall), then keeps holding it and glides.

Lesson 6 of 20 · 50 minutes

Tiles and the map editor

Draw ground tiles, mark the solid ones with a sprite flag, and paint the first level in TIC-80's map editor.

In this lesson

  • tiles and the TILES tab
  • sprite flags
  • the map editor and its tools
  • the world view
  • drawing the map with map()
  • the transparent color in the map

Starting point: lesson05.png · Finished: lesson06.png · Play it

Step 1 Draw the ground tiles

A level is built from tiles: 8 x 8 pictures on the TILES tab (numbers 0-255), laid out on a grid called the map. Tile 0 stays empty: an empty map cell shows nothing.

The sprite sheet has two halves, and the sprite editor shows one at a time: the two small tabs left of the sheet (or Tab) switch between them. So when you switch to TILES, Pip isn't gone: it's still on the SPRITES half, at 256. The map can only use the TILES half.

Draw these tiles, numbers 1 to 6, on the TILES tab:

The grass tiles go on the top row of the ground, the dirt tiles below. The edge versions round off the corners where the ground ends. A quick way: draw the left end (1) first. Copy it (CtrlC), click slot 2 and paste (CtrlV), then change the pixels that differ to make the middle. The right end (3) is the left end's mirror image: paste tile 1 into slot 3, click FLIP HORZ (under the canvas), and fix a few specks. The dirt goes the same way: 4, then a copy of it for 5, then a copy of 5 for 6.

Then some decorations: a bush (24), a flower (25), tall grass (26) and a fence (28).

Use color 0 for the sky parts of a tile, like above the grass blades. When the map is drawn with color 0 as transparent, the background shows through.

Step 2 Mark the solid tiles with a flag

Pip will soon stand on the ground and bump into walls (lesson 7). The code needs to know which tiles are solid. TIC-80 gives every sprite and tile 8 flags, on/off switches with no fixed meaning: your game decides what they mean.

In Pip's Peak, flag 0 means solid.

Switch on the advanced view (the small button at the top left of the sprite editor). A column of 8 small boxes appears next to the canvas: the flags of the selected tile. Select each of tiles 1-6 and make sure box 0 is on: click it if it isn't. (If you drew along with the pictures above, it already is.)

Leave the decorations without flags: Pip walks in front of them.

Check

Run it (CtrlR): the game is still lesson 5's, green ground and all. Now ask the cart about the flags: press Esc (more than once if needed) until you see the console, and type eval trace(fget(2, 0)). eval runs a line of Lua in the cart, and trace prints its value: true, tile 2 has flag 0. eval trace(fget(24, 0)) prints false: the bush has no flag. If a tile gives the wrong answer, fix its flag box and run it again: the console sees the flags the cart had when it last ran.

Step 3 Paint the map

Press F3 for the map editor. The map is a huge grid of 240 x 136 cells, each holding one tile number. One screen shows 30 x 17 cells (240 / 8 and 136 / 8).

Press Shift to open the tile sheet and click a tile: the sheet closes by itself, and you paint that tile with the mouse. (Drag across several tiles in the sheet to paint a whole block of them at once.)

The tools on the right of the top bar: draw (1, the default), drag (2, moves the view), select (3: drag a rectangle, then CtrlC copies it and CtrlV pastes a copy you click into place), fill (4). The grid button (or the key left of 1) shows the cell borders. To find a cell, hover over the map with the draw tool: a little box next to the cursor shows the cell under it as column:row, like 013:011. To pick up a tile that's already in the map, click it with the middle mouse button.

Paint the first screen of Green Meadow at the top left of the map, cells 0-29 across and 0-16 down:

  • Rows 14, 15 and 16 are the ground: grass tiles on row 14, dirt below. The ground runs on past both sides of this screen, so here it's all middle tiles; the edge tiles are for where the ground ends: at the gaps, and at the hills and rocks on the later screens.
  • A floating platform of grass on row 11, columns 13-17: tiles 1 2 2 2 3 (the grass with its two rounded ends).
  • A few bushes, flowers and tall grass on row 13, just above the ground.

The whole level is four screens wide (120 cells).

You can paint all four screens now, or just the first one and then take the whole map from the lesson cart: type load lesson06.png map in the console, which copies only the map into your cart (Loading a lesson cart). It replaces your whole map, your first screen too, with the lesson's. Lesson 9 needs the full map.

To move around the map, drag with the right mouse button, or press Tab for the world view, which shows the whole map with one pixel per cell; gray lines mark the screens:

Your first screen is in the top-left corner of the world view. If you loaded the map, the other three screens run on to its right.

Explore the map in the Map Lab: the real map editor, with this lesson's map. Point at a cell to find out what is in it and whether Pip can stand on it, jump around with the small map of the whole world, paint, and ▶ Try it in the game. Its Sprites tab shows the tiles and their flags.

Step 4 Draw the map in the game

Change the drawing part of TIC(): instead of the green rectangle, draw the map.

map(x, y, w, h, sx, sy, colorkey) draws w x h map cells, starting at map cell x, y, at screen position sx, sy. Here: 30 x 17 cells from the top-left corner of the map, drawn at the top-left of the screen. The last argument makes color 0 transparent, so the sky shows through the empty parts of tiles.

Check your work

The first screen of Green Meadow appears: ground at the bottom, the floating platform, decorations. Pip still stands on the ground, but walks straight through the floating platform when it jumps, and walks off the right edge of the screen. The next lesson fixes both.

Challenge A second platform

Add another floating platform on screen 1 of the map, two rows above the first one.

See what it might look like

A second grass platform (tiles 1 2 2 2 3) on row 9, columns 19-23, two rows above the first. Jump with Z under them: Pip goes right through the first one and pokes its head into the second, because nothing in the code knows they are solid yet.

Challenge Your own tile

Draw a stone block tile, give it flag 0, and build a little wall with it.

See what it might look like

Tile 35 is a gray stone block with flag 0 switched on, stacked into a wall two blocks wide and three high right of the floating platform. Pip still walks through it here: flag 0 starts to matter in lesson 7.

Challenge Night map

Use lesson 4's palette changes to give the meadow a night look. Pip changes color too, because it shares those palette colors with the grass: which colors can you change so that Pip stays the same?

See what it might look like

BOOT() changes three colors: 10 (the sky) and 2 and 1 (the dirt). Pip is drawn only with colors 3, 4, 5, 6 and 15, so it looks the same as by day; the grass stays bright because its greens (5 and 6) are Pip's too.

Lesson 7 of 20 · 50 minutes

Tile collision

Make the map solid. Pip stands on the ground, bumps its head and is stopped by walls, using the flags from lesson 6.

In this lesson

  • hitboxes
  • reading the map with mget and flags with fget
  • checking a box against tiles
  • moving one axis at a time
  • snapping to the tile edge
  • sub-pixel positions

Starting point: lesson06.png · Finished: lesson07.png · Play it

Step 1 Give Pip a hitbox

Collision works with boxes. Pip's box is 6 pixels wide and 8 tall: a little narrower than the sprite, which feels fairer (Pip doesn't catch on corners with empty pixels). x, y is now the box's top-left corner, and the sprite is drawn one pixel to its left.

New and changed definitions outside the functions (constants, tables, variables): add these to your cart, or replace the old version of the same lines.

Pip starts in the air at x = 16, y = 80, and falls onto the grass. Keep GROUND_Y for now: the landing code in update_player still reads it, until you replace that function below.

In draw_player, the sprite is now drawn at p.x - 1:

Check

Run it (CtrlR): Pip now starts near the left edge, up in the air, and drops onto the grass.

Step 2 Ask the map what is solid

mget(x, y) returns the tile number in map cell x, y. fget(tile, flag) returns whether that tile has a flag switched on. Together:

To test a whole box, check every map cell it touches. A cell is 8 pixels, so pixel x is in cell x // 8:

Pip's box is never bigger than a tile, so it touches at most 2 x 2 cells; but this function works for boxes of any size, like the boss in lesson 19.

Check

Nothing calls these two yet, so ask them in the console. Run it, then press Esc until you see the console:

  • eval trace(solid_at(0, 14)) prints true: cell 0, 14 is grass.
  • eval trace(solid_at(0, 0)) prints false: sky.
  • eval trace(box_hits(16, 108, 6, 8)) prints true: a box that low pokes into the ground.

Step 3 Move, then push back out

The trick that makes platformer collision simple: move one axis at a time. First move sideways, and if the box is now inside a wall, push it back out to the side. Then do the same up and down. Because only one axis moved, you know which way to push.

If Pip moved right into a wall, its right edge (x + w - 1) is in the wall's cell; // 8 * 8 rounds down to that cell's left edge, and subtracting the width puts Pip right next to the wall. Moving left, Pip goes to the right edge of the cell it entered.

The same idea vertically: falling into the ground puts Pip's feet on top of the tile, jumping into a ceiling puts its head just under it.

Check

Run it, press Esc until you see the console, and try a box that falls 8 pixels into the ground: eval e={x=16,y=100,w=6,h=8} trace(move_y(e,8)) trace(e.y). It prints true (it hit something) and 104: pushed back up to stand on the grass.

Step 4 Use it in update_player

  • Sideways movement now goes through move_x(p, dx).
  • p.x = math.max(0, math.min(p.x, 240 - p.w)) keeps Pip on the screen (until lesson 9 adds scrolling).
  • After moving vertically, p.ground comes from looking one pixel below Pip's feet. Positions are fractions (gravity adds 0.25 at a time), and asking "is there ground right below?" is more reliable than remembering whether the last move hit something.
  • When standing, the fraction gravity added is dropped (p.y // 1), so Pip stands exactly on the tile.
  • Falling off the bottom of the screen puts Pip back at the start.

Now nothing uses GROUND_Y: delete it.

Check your work

Pip falls and lands on the grass. Jumping under the floating platform, it bumps its head. You can jump onto the platform, walk along it and fall off the end.

If Pip sinks into the ground or floats above it, check the flags: the grass and dirt tiles need flag 0, and only those. Check them from the console as in lesson 6: run the game, press Esc until you see the console, and type eval trace(fget(2, 0)): true if tile 2 has flag 0.

Challenge Walls

Paint a wall, three tiles high, on the first screen. Make sure Pip can't walk through it, but can jump over it.

See what it might look like

A wall of ground tiles on columns 6-7, rows 11-13 (1 3 on top, 4 6 below): 24 pixels high, lower than Pip's 30-pixel jump. Walk into it with Right, then jump onto it and over it with Z.

Challenge Ceilings everywhere

What happens if you jump while standing directly under the platform? Follow the code through move_y with a negative dy to explain it.

See what it might look like

Nothing to change, just watch: jumping makes dy negative, so move_y moves Pip's box up into the platform. box_hits finds a solid tile there, so move_y puts Pip just under it and returns true, and update_player sets vy to 0: Pip falls back down. Stand under the platform and press Z.

Challenge A pit

Remove a few ground tiles to make a hole (and use the edge tiles on both sides of it). Pip should fall in and start again at the beginning. Does this need any new code? Look at the end of update_player.

See what it might look like

Columns 22-24 of the ground are empty, with edge tiles (3 and 6, 1 and 4) on both sides; the code needs no change, because update_player already sends Pip back to the start once it falls below the screen (y > 136). Walk right into the hole to try it.

 local SPR_JUMP, SPR_FALL = 262, 263
 
-local GROUND_Y = 104    -- Pip stands on the map's grass (row 14 starts at y = 112)
-local GRAVITY = 0.25    -- added to vy every frame (pixels per frame per frame)
-local JUMP_SPEED = -4   -- vy when a jump starts (negative is up)
-local JUMP_CUT = -1.5   -- releasing the button early caps vy here
-local MAX_FALL = 4      -- the fastest Pip can fall
+local F_SOLID = 0       -- sprite flag 0 marks tiles you can stand on
+
+local GRAVITY = 0.25
+local JUMP_SPEED = -4
+local JUMP_CUT = -1.5
+local MAX_FALL = 4
+local START_X, START_Y = 16, 80
 
 -- == State ==
+-- x, y is the top-left corner of Pip's hitbox, a 6x8 box (the sprite is
+-- drawn one pixel to the left so the box sits in the middle of it)
 player = {
-  x = 116, y = GROUND_Y, vy = 0,
-  flip = 0, moving = false,
-  ground = true, jumping = false
+  x = START_X, y = START_Y, w = 6,
+  h = 8, vy = 0, flip = 0,
+  moving = false, ground = false,
+  jumping = false
 }
 t = 0
+
+-- == Collision ==
+-- Is the map tile at cell (tx, ty) solid?
+function solid_at(tx, ty)
+  return fget(mget(tx, ty), F_SOLID)
+end
+
+-- Does a w x h box at pixel (x, y) overlap any solid tile?
+function box_hits(x, y, w, h)
+  for ty = y // 8, (y + h - 1) // 8 do
+    for tx = x // 8,
+        (x + w - 1) // 8 do
+      if solid_at(tx, ty) then
+        return true
+      end
+    end
+  end
+  return false
+end
+
+-- Move e sideways by dx; if that runs into a wall, push it back out.
+-- Returns true when it hit something.
+function move_x(e, dx)
+  e.x = e.x + dx
+  if not box_hits(e.x, e.y, e.w, e.h)
+  then
+    return false
+  end
+  if dx > 0 then
+    e.x =
+      (e.x + e.w - 1) // 8 * 8 - e.w   -- just left of the wall
+  else
+    e.x = e.x // 8 * 8 + 8                  -- just right of the wall
+  end
+  return true
+end
+
+-- Move e up or down by dy, the same way.
+function move_y(e, dy)
+  e.y = e.y + dy
+  if not box_hits(e.x, e.y, e.w, e.h)

Lesson 8 of 20 · 45 minutes

Game feel

Make Pip pleasant to control with acceleration and friction, coyote time, a jump buffer and a squash on hard landings.

In this lesson

  • horizontal velocity, acceleration and friction
  • collecting tuning values in one table
  • coyote time
  • jump buffering
  • squash on landing

Starting point: lesson07.png · Finished: lesson08.png · Play it

Step 1 Collect the tuning values

"Game feel" is how a game responds to your hands. It comes from many small numbers, so put them all in one table where they're easy to find and change:

New and changed definitions outside the functions (constants, tables, variables): add these to your cart, or replace the old version of the same lines.

Keep the old GRAVITY, JUMP_SPEED, JUMP_CUT and MAX_FALL for now: update_player still reads them until the next steps change it to P.gravity, P.jump_speed and so on.

Check

Run it (CtrlR): nothing changes yet, but there's no error.

Step 2 Speed up and slow down

The next three steps change update_player piece by piece.

Until now Pip moved exactly one pixel per frame or not at all. Real movement has horizontal velocity vx that changes gradually. This helper moves a value toward a target by at most a step:

Holding a direction moves vx toward the run speed; letting go moves it toward 0. On the ground the changes are quick, in the air slower (you steer less in mid-air):

p.flip = dir < 0 and 1 or 0 is Lua's short way of writing "1 if dir < 0, otherwise 0".

Check

Run it: hold Right and Pip takes a moment to reach full speed. Let go and it slides a little before it stops. Jumping works as before.

Step 3 Coyote time and the jump buffer

Two invisible helpers make jumping feel fair:

  • Coyote time: for a few frames after running off a ledge, you can still jump. Without it, players press jump a frame too late and feel cheated.
  • Jump buffer: if you press jump a few frames before landing, the jump happens when you land. Without it, early presses are lost.

Both are counters:

p.coyote is reset to 6 every frame Pip is on the ground and counts down in the air; p.buffer is set to 6 on a press and counts down. A jump happens when both are above zero.

Check

Run it: get onto the floating platform, walk off its end and press Z just after you leave it: Pip still jumps. Press Z just before you land, and the jump happens as soon as Pip touches the ground.

Step 4 Squash on landing

Draw one more frame: Pip squashed flat, for hard landings.

Remember how fast Pip was falling, and if it lands from a fast fall (a full jump is fast enough; a short hop isn't), show the squash frame for a few frames: p.squash counts down from 6.

In draw_player, the squash frame comes first:

Now nothing reads the old GRAVITY, JUMP_SPEED, JUMP_CUT and MAX_FALL: remove them.

Check

Run it: take a full jump (hold Z) and Pip squashes flat for a moment when it lands. Even the drop at the start squashes it. A short hop doesn't.

Step 5 All of update_player

Here is update_player in one piece. One change at the bottom is new: falling off the screen now also sets p.vx back to 0.

Check your work

Pip takes a moment to reach full speed and slides a little when you let go. You can still jump just after running off the platform's edge, and a jump pressed just before landing still happens. A jump from the platform ends in a squash.

Challenge Tune it

Change one value in P at a time and feel the difference: friction = 0.05 (ice), air_accel = 0 (no steering in the air), coyote = 1 or buffer = 1 (no help at all; 0 would stop every jump, because a jump needs both counts above 0). Then choose your favorite values.

Challenge Dash

Pressing X (button 5) gives Pip a burst of speed (vx = 4 in the direction it faces) that friction then slows down. Allow one dash until Pip touches the ground again.

Hint

approach slows vx down only toward the run speed when a direction is held, so for a dash skip the acceleration for a few frames: add a dash counter.

See what it might look like

X sets vx to 4 in the direction Pip faces, and for 8 frames (the dash counter) the arrows are ignored, so only friction slows Pip down. Dash from standing still, then jump with Z and dash in mid-air: a second X before landing does nothing.

Lesson 9 of 20 · 40 minutes

The camera and scrolling

Let the level be bigger than the screen. A camera follows Pip through all four screens of Green Meadow, with hills scrolling slower behind it.

In this lesson

  • world coordinates and screen coordinates
  • a camera that follows and stops at the level's edges
  • drawing the map with an offset
  • parallax backgrounds
  • walls at the level's edges

Starting point: lesson08.png · Finished: lesson09.png · Play it

Step 1 Describe the level

This lesson scrolls through all of Green Meadow, so your map needs all four screens of it now. If you painted only the first, copy the rest from the lesson cart: load lesson09.png map in the console (see Loading a lesson cart).

The level is the rectangle of the map it occupies, in cells. Green Meadow starts at cell 0, 0 and is 120 cells wide and 17 tall:

Add clouds to the sky too: draw tiles 29-31 and paint a few clouds in the top rows of the map.

Check

Run it (CtrlR): the clouds you painted on the first screen float in the sky. Nothing else changes yet.

Step 2 Positions in the world, positions on the screen

So far Pip's position was its position on the screen. Now there are two kinds:

  • World coordinates: where something is in the level. Pip can be at x = 700.
  • Screen coordinates: where it appears, 0 to 239.

The camera is the world position of the screen's top-left corner. To draw anything: screen = world - camera.

Step 3 Follow Pip, but stay inside the level

The camera tries to put Pip in the middle of the screen (player.x + 3 - 120), but clamp keeps it between the level's left edge and its right edge minus one screen, so you never see past the end of the level. // 1 rounds down to whole pixels, so the map doesn't shimmer.

Check

Nothing calls update_camera yet, so try it in the console. Run it, press Esc until you see the console, and put Pip far into the level: eval player.x=400 update_camera() trace(cam.x) prints 283 (400 + 3 - 120). eval trace(clamp(-50, 0, 720)) prints 0: -50 is below the range, so clamp gives its lowest value. Run it again afterwards to put Pip back at the start.

Step 4 Parallax hills

Things far away move slower when you move. Drawing hills that scroll at a quarter and at half the camera's speed gives the level depth:

far % 96 makes the hills repeat every 96 pixels, so a few circles cover a level of any width. The circles reach below the bottom of the screen, so the hills fill the pits too: looking into a pit, you see the hills far below.

Step 5 Draw everything relative to the camera

The map: draw the cells under the screen, and shift them by the part of the camera position that isn't a whole cell:

Why 31 x 18 cells and not 30 x 17? When the camera is at x = 3, the first cell is shifted 3 pixels left and the screen needs one more column on the right to fill the gap.

Pip, in draw_player, subtracts the camera too:

Check

Run it and hold Right: once Pip reaches the middle of the screen, the ground scrolls and Pip stays in the middle, with the hills drifting slower behind it. Pip still stops after a while: the old "stay on the screen" line keeps it inside the first 240 pixels of the level.

Step 6 Walls at the level's edges, and falling out

Pip shouldn't be able to walk off the level. Treating every cell left and right of the level as solid does it with one line in solid_at:

The old "stay on the screen" line in update_player goes: delete the two lines after move_x that start p.x = math.max(0, and math.min(p.x, 240 - p.w)). Falling now means falling below the level's bottom edge. At the end of update_player:

Check your work

Run right: the camera follows, the far hills creep along, the near hills move faster, the ground fastest. At the end of the level, the camera stops and Pip walks up to an invisible wall. Falling into the first gap, on screen 2, sends Pip back to the start.

Challenge Look ahead

When Pip runs right, it's more useful to see what's coming. Move the camera target 32 pixels in the direction Pip faces.

Hint

Use player.flip: local ahead = player.flip == 0 and 32 or -32, and add it to the target before clamping. To make the camera glide instead of jumping when Pip turns, move cam.x part of the way to the target each frame: cam.x = cam.x + (target - cam.x) * 0.1. That makes cam.x a fraction again, so round it where you use it for drawing (cam.x // 1), or the map shakes by a pixel.

See what it might look like

The camera's target is 32 pixels ahead of Pip, on the side it faces, and cam.x moves a tenth of the way there each frame, so the view glides over when Pip turns around. Run right, then turn left, and watch Pip drift to the other side of the screen.

Challenge A third layer

Add a sun or a moon that doesn't move at all, drawn after cls and before the hills.

See what it might look like

A yellow sun, circ(200, 24, 10, 4), drawn right after cls in draw_background: it uses no camera position, so it stays put while the hills and the ground scroll past. Run right to see the three layers move at three speeds.

Lesson 10 of 20 · 45 minutes

Game states and the level loader

Give the game a title screen, and let the map itself say where things start, using marker tiles and a level loader.

In this lesson

  • game states
  • a level table
  • marker tiles
  • a loader that scans the map
  • restoring the map with sync
  • functions stored in a table

Starting point: lesson09.png · Finished: lesson10.png · Play it

Step 1 Draw a start marker

Instead of writing Pip's start position in the code, mark it in the map. Draw tile 50, a little Pip-shaped marker (it's only seen in the map editor), and an arrow sign (34) as a decoration:

In the map editor, put tile 50 where Pip should start: column 1, row 13 of Green Meadow. Put the arrow sign at column 5, row 13.

When a level starts, a loader scans the level's cells. Every marker tile it recognizes is replaced by an empty cell and does something: here, "Pip starts here".

Check

Run it (CtrlR): the start marker and the arrow sign show in Green Meadow as ordinary tiles, next to where Pip starts. The loader will hide the marker.

Step 2 A table of levels

Levels become entries in a list, each with its rectangle on the map and its colors. Keep LEVEL, SKY, START_X and START_Y for now: the functions still use them.

New and changed definitions outside the functions (constants, tables, variables): add these to your cart, or replace the old version of the same lines.

And a few globals describe where the game is. Put them below LEVELS: lvl starts as its first level.

Check

Run it: Pip now drops in at the far left edge of the level and lands on the ground. Pip's new table starts it at 0, 0, and nothing reads the start marker yet.

lvl is the current level's table, so lvl.w is its width. Replace every LEVEL in these functions with lvl, and SKY with lvl.sky:

Check

Run it: nothing changes, and there's no error.

Falling out of the level will put Pip back at the start with this function:

Call it at the end of update_player:

Now nothing uses LEVEL, SKY, START_X and START_Y: delete them.

Check

Run it, then fall into a pit: Pip drops in at the left edge again.

Step 3 Spawn functions

In Lua, functions are values: you can store them in a table. SPAWN maps a marker tile number to the function that handles it:

The function gets the marker's pixel position. For the start marker it remembers where Pip begins (one pixel in, to center the 6-pixel box in the 8-pixel cell).

Step 4 The loader

  • sync(4, 0, false) copies the map from the cart back into memory. The loader changes the map (mset replaces markers), so without this, a second visit to the level would find the markers gone. The 4 means "the map" (see the sync masks in the API reference).
  • The two loops visit every cell of the level. SPAWN[mget(tx, ty)] is nil for normal tiles, and a function for markers.
  • mset(tx, ty, 0) empties the cell, so the marker is never drawn in the game.

Check

Run it: nothing changes yet, because nothing calls load_level. Press Esc until you see the console and type eval load_level(1) trace(start_x .. "," .. start_y). It prints 9,104: the marker at column 1, row 13, plus one pixel.

Step 5 Game states

A real game is more than its level: a title screen, the game, later a game-over screen. Each is a state with its own update and draw functions.

The game itself moves into update_play and draw_play (level_t counts the frames since the level started, for the banner):

The level's name appears for two seconds at the start:

For now, make TIC run only the game:

Check

Run it: "GREEN MEADOW" shows for two seconds, then the game plays as before. Pip still starts at the left edge, and the marker still shows, because nothing calls load_level yet.

Now the title screen. This helper centers text, so you don't work out each line's x position by hand: print returns the width of the text it drew, so it prints the text once far above the screen (where it can't be seen) to measure it, then again at the right place:

print(text, x, y, color, fixed, scale): scale 3 draws the title text three times as big. Drawing it twice, offset by 2 pixels in a dark color, gives it a shadow. t // 30 % 2 == 0 is true for half a second, false for the next half: blinking.

Check

Run it: nothing changes, and there's no error.

Z on the title screen loads the level and starts the game:

TIC() runs the current state. Replace your TIC with this one:

Check your work

The game starts on the title screen. Z starts Green Meadow with Pip at the start marker, and the level's name shows for two seconds. The marker itself is not visible in the game.

Challenge A pause state

Add a "pause" state: X (button 5) in the game switches to it, and X again back to "play". Draw the game with "PAUSED" on top, and don't update anything while paused.

Hint

In TIC(): elseif state == "pause" then update_pause() draw_play() print("PAUSED", 100, 60, 12) end. t keeps counting in TIC, so Pip's animation would keep playing: only count it when the state isn't "pause".

See what it might look like

X switches between the "play" and "pause" states; while paused, TIC() only draws the game with "PAUSED" on top, and the frame counter t stops too, so even Pip's run animation freezes. Start with Z, run, and press X in mid-jump.

Challenge A second start

Make a tiny test level somewhere else on the map (one screen, with its own start marker), add it to LEVELS, and load it with A on the title screen. The A key is button 6 (btnp(6)), not the game's BTN_A, which is button 4, the Z key.

Lesson 11 of 20 · 50 minutes

Collectibles, entities and the HUD

Add spinning coins and hidden gems with an entity system, and show the score in a status bar.

In this lesson

  • entities (tables with update and draw functions)
  • removing items from a list while going through it
  • box overlap
  • particles
  • a HUD with string.format

Starting point: lesson10.png · Finished: lesson11.png · Play it

Step 1 Draw the coins and gems

A spinning coin is four frames: the coin seen from the front, turned a little, edge-on, then turned a little the other way. Draw them on the SPRITES tab at 288-291 and the gem at 292. Then draw the markers on the TILES tab, so you can place coins and gems in the map: tile 48 looks like a coin and tile 49 like a gem. And back on the SPRITES tab, two small icons for the status bar: 354 (coin) and 355 (gem).

In the map editor, place coin markers along Green Meadow: a row of three over the floating platform, an arc over the first gap, an arc that shows the jump off the end of the big rock, and so on. Hide three gems in hard-to-reach places. The finished level has one high above the first floating platform (column 15, row 7), one in the tunnel under the big rock on screen 3 (75, 12) and one high over the last gap between the pillars on screen 4 (107, 6), where only a well-timed jump gets it without falling in. To use the finished level's coins and gems instead, draw tiles 48 and 49 and type load lesson11.png map in the console (Loading a lesson cart).

Check

Run it (CtrlR) and press Z: the coin and gem markers show in Green Meadow as plain, still tiles. Pip walks through them.

Step 2 Entities

Give coins, and everything else in the level that isn't Pip or the map, the same shape: an entity is a table with a box (x, y, w, h) and two functions, update and draw. A list, ents, holds them all.

New and changed definitions outside the functions (constants, tables, variables): add these to your cart, or replace the old version of the same lines.

Check

Run it: nothing changes, and there's no error.

When an entity sets e.dead = true, it's removed from the list. Removing an entry shifts the ones after it down by one, so the loop goes backwards: removing entry 5 then doesn't skip the entry that moved into slot 5.

ipairs goes through a list in order, giving the index (ignored here with _) and the entry.

Step 3 Touching: do two boxes overlap?

Two boxes overlap when each one starts before the other one ends, both across and down.

Check

Run it, press Esc until you see the console and type eval trace(overlaps({x=0,y=0,w=8,h=8}, {x=4,y=4,w=8,h=8})): it prints true. Change the second box's x=4,y=4 to x=8,y=0: false, because the boxes only touch.

Step 4 Coins and gems

They name update_pickup, draw_coin and draw_gem, which come later. That's fine: nothing calls those yet.

Tell the loader about the markers. SPAWN must come after new_coin and new_gem in your cart: the table is built when the cart starts, so a function further down isn't there yet and SPAWN stores nil (nothing spawns, and there's no error). If your new functions are at the bottom of your cart, put SPAWN below them. (The label shows where it is in the lesson's cart.)

and clear the entities and particles when a level loads, before the loop that spawns the new ones:

Check

Run it and press Z: the coin and gem markers are gone. The loader turns them into entities, but nothing draws those yet. Press Esc until you see the console and type eval trace(#ents): it prints how many coins and gems you placed. If it prints 0, your SPAWN is above new_coin: move it down.

The gem bobs: math.sin(t / 10) swings smoothly between -1 and 1, times 2 pixels.

Add draw_ents() to draw_play, after the map(...) line.

Check

Run it and press Z: the coins spin and the gems bob, but Pip passes through them.

Step 5 Picking up and particles

Coins and gems use the same update function. When Pip touches the pickup, it's removed and counted:

Its sparkles are particles: dots that fly for a moment and disappear. burst throws n of them in random directions:

math.random() returns a number between 0 and 1, so math.random() * 2 - 1 is between -1 and 1. vy + 0.1 makes the dots fall.

Add update_ents() and update_parts() to update_play, after update_player(player).

Check

Run it, press Z and walk into a coin: it vanishes (the sparkles aren't drawn yet). Press Esc until you see the console and type eval trace(score): 10 for each coin you took.

Step 6 The HUD

The HUD (heads-up display) is the bar that shows the score. It's drawn after the level and Pip, on top of them, and not relative to the camera:

string.format("%06d", score) writes the score with six digits, padded with zeros: 000120. The true argument to print uses fixed-width digits, so the numbers don't jiggle as they change.

Particles are drawn as single pixels:

Starting a game sets the counters back to zero, in update_title:

Finally, draw_play draws the particles after Pip, then the HUD, then the level banner. Here are update_play and draw_play with all the new calls:

Check your work

Coins spin; touching one makes it sparkle away and adds 10 to the score and 1 to the coins. A gem adds 500. The counters show in a black bar at the top. Coins you took stay gone, even after falling into a pit; restarting the game (CtrlR) brings them back.

Challenge Big coins

See what it might look like

Tile 61 is a big-coin marker: the coin is drawn at scale 2 with a 12x12 box, and touching it adds 5 coins. Jump into the one after the floating platform with Z.

Challenge Magnet

Hint

In update_pickup, compute dx = player.x - e.x, dy = player.y - e.y; if both are small, add a fraction of them to e.x and e.y.

See what it might look like

Coins closer than 24 pixels across and down slide toward Pip, an eighth of the way each frame. Stop at the edge of the gap: the coins above it fly over to Pip.

Challenge Coin total

See what it might look like

@@ -112,4 +120,124 @@
   end
   return true
+end
+
+-- == Entities ==
+-- An entity is a table with a box (x, y, w, h) and two functions:
+-- update(e) runs every frame, draw(e) draws it. Setting e.dead = true
+-- removes it.
+function add_ent(e)
+  ents[#ents + 1] = e
+  return e
+end
+
+-- Do two boxes overlap?
+function overlaps(a, b)
+  return a.x < b.x + b.w
+    and b.x < a.x + a.w and a.y < b.y
+    + b.h and b.y < a.y + a.h
+end
+
+function update_ents()
+  -- walk the list backwards so removing an entry doesn't skip the next one
+  for i = #ents, 1, -1 do
+    local e = ents[i]
+    e.update(e)
+    if e.dead then
+      table.remove(ents, i)
+    end
+  end
+end
+
+function draw_ents()
+  for _, e in ipairs(ents) do
+    e.draw(e)
+  end
+end
+
+-- == Particles ==
+function burst(x, y, n, color)
+  for _ = 1, n do
+    parts[#parts + 1] = {
+      x = x, y = y,
+      vx = math.random() * 2 - 1,
+      vy = math.random() * -2,
+      life = 20 + math.random(10),
+      color = color
+    }
+  end
+end
+
+function update_parts()
+  for i = #parts, 1, -1 do
+    local d = parts[i]
+    d.x, d.y, d.vy = d.x + d.vx,
+      d.y + d.vy, d.vy + 0.1
+    d.life = d.life - 1
+    if d.life <= 0 then
+      table.remove(parts, i)
+    end
+  end
+end
+
+function draw_parts()
+  for _, d in ipairs(parts) do
+    pix(d.x - cam.x, d.y - cam.y,
+        d.color)
+  end
+end
+
+-- == Pickups ==
+function new_coin(x, y)
+  add_ent({
+    x = x + 1, y = y + 1, w = 6,
+    h = 6, update = update_pickup,
+    draw = draw_coin, kind = "coin"
+  })
+end
+
+function new_gem(x, y)
+  add_ent({
+    x = x + 1, y = y + 1, w = 6,
+    h = 6, update = update_pickup,
+    draw = draw_gem, kind = "gem"
+  })
+end
+
+function update_pickup(e)
+  if overlaps(player, e) then
+    e.dead = true
+    if e.kind == "coin" then
+      coins = coins + 1
+      score = score + 10
+      burst(e.x + 3, e.y + 3, 6, 4)
+    else
+      gems = gems + 1
+      score = score + 500
+      burst(e.x + 3, e.y + 3, 12, 11)
+    end
+  end
+end
+
+function draw_coin(e)
+  spr(anim_frame(ANIM_COIN, 8), e.x
+      - 1 - cam.x, e.y - 1 - cam.y, 0)
+end
+
+function draw_gem(e)
+  local bob =
+    math.sin(t / 10) * 2 // 1   -- float up and down
+  spr(SPR_GEM, e.x - 1 - cam.x,
+      e.y - 1 - cam.y + bob, 0)
+end
+
+-- == HUD ==
+function draw_hud()
+  rect(0, 0, 240, 9, 0)
+  print(string.format("%06d", score),
+      4, 2, 12, true)
+  spr(SPR_HUD_COIN, 46, 0, 0)
+  print("x" .. coins, 55, 2, 12, true)
+  spr(SPR_HUD_GEM, 80, 0, 0)
+  print(gems .. "/3", 89, 2, 12, true)
 end

Lesson 12 of 20 · 50 minutes

Hazards, health and checkpoints

Add spikes that hurt, three hearts, lives, checkpoints to come back to, and a game-over screen.

In this lesson

  • a second sprite flag for hazards
  • health and invulnerability
  • knockback
  • checkpoints
  • a "dead" state
  • game over

Starting point: lesson11.png · Finished: lesson12.png · Play it

Step 1 Draw spikes, a checkpoint and the hearts

Give the spikes tile (13) flag 1: in this game flag 1 means hurts. Then draw tile 51, the checkpoint marker (a flag on a pole), so you can place checkpoints in the map.

In the map editor, put two spike tiles on the ground of screen 2 (columns 53 and 54, row 13) and a checkpoint marker at the start of screen 3 (column 60, row 13).

Check

Run it (CtrlR) and press Z: the spikes and the checkpoint marker sit in the level. Pip walks right through the spikes: they don't hurt yet. Press Esc until you see the console: eval trace(fget(13, 1)) prints true.

Step 2 Health and lives

New and changed definitions outside the functions (constants, tables, variables): add these to your cart, or replace the old version of the same lines.

MAX_HP goes with the other constants at the top: player uses it for hp, so it has to come first.

Pip has three hearts (hp). Losing all of them costs a life, and losing all lives is game over. After a hit, Pip is invulnerable for 90 frames (a second and a half) and blinks, so one spike can't take all three hearts at once.

The HUD shows the hearts and lives:

Check

Run it and press Z: the HUD shows three red hearts and Pip's head with x3.

Step 3 Getting hurt

The knockback pushes Pip away from the hit (left if the hit came from the right) and a little up. Falling into a pit doesn't take a heart: it loses a life right away.

lose_life changes the state with set_state, which also resets a timer, state_t, so each state knows how long it has been running. It also stops the blinking, so Pip stays visible as it falls. Replace every state = "play" (in update_title) with set_state("play"):

Check

Run it: Z starts the game as before. Nothing calls hurt or lose_life yet, but there's no error.

Step 4 Touching a hazard

This is like box_hits, for any flag, and without the level walls:

In update_player:

The hazard test uses a slightly smaller box than Pip's (one pixel in from each side, two from the top), so brushing a spike with the edge of Pip's sprite doesn't count. It still tests whole tiles, not the spike's pixels. A spike hits Pip from the way it is facing, so Pip is knocked backwards.

Check

Run it: walk into the spikes. A heart goes empty and Pip is pushed back and up. Touching them again straight away does nothing for a moment (the blinking comes later).

On the third hit, or a fall into the first gap, the lives go to x2 and the game stops. That's expected: Pip is in the "dead" state now, and TIC doesn't run it yet. Step 6, New states, fixes it.

Step 5 Checkpoints

A checkpoint is an entity that, when touched, moves the respawn point. Put these three functions above SPAWN, like the coin and gem ones:

Check

Run it: the checkpoint at the start of screen 3 shows its flag down. Touch it: the flag goes up with a burst of sparks. To get there, hop over the spikes and let go of Right so Pip lands on the ground before the gap, then jump the gap. If Pip lands past the flag, walk back to it. A fall still stops the game, as in check 4: run it again. (If the marker tile still shows, your checkpoint functions are below SPAWN.)

Step 6 New states: dead and game over

After losing a life, Pip hops up and falls off the screen, and 90 frames later comes back at the last checkpoint, or the game is over:

Check

Run it: nothing changes yet (a fall into the first gap still stops the game), but there's no error.

TIC counts state_t up every frame and runs the new states. The dead state keeps drawing the level, so Pip can be seen falling:

reset_player also refills the hearts and clears the blinking:

Check

Run it: fall into the first gap. Pip hops, falls off the screen, and comes back at the start with full hearts and x2. Touch the checkpoint, then fall again: Pip comes back at the flag. Lose the last life and you get GAME OVER with your score; Z goes back to the title.

Step 7 Blinking

While invulnerable, draw_player skips drawing every other 4 frames (blinking), and shows the hurt sprite for the first 20 frames after a hit:

Check your work

Pip now blinks after a hit and shows the hurt face. Spikes take one heart, push Pip back and make it blink; touching them again while blinking does nothing. Three hits, or a fall into a gap, lose a life: Pip hops and falls, then comes back at the start, or at the checkpoint once you have touched it. After the last life, the game-over screen shows the score; Z goes back to the title.

Challenge Hearts to find

Add a heart marker that gives back one heart (up to MAX_HP) when touched.

See what it might look like

Tile 62 is a heart marker; touching the heart gives back one heart, never more than MAX_HP. One takes the place of a coin over the spikes after the hill: jump over the spikes with Z to take it.

Challenge Ceiling spikes

Make a hazard tile that only hurts when Pip touches it from below, like spikes on a ceiling. (Draw upside-down spikes with the sprite editor's flip button.)

See what it might look like

Tile 35 is the spikes tile flipped upside down, with flags 0 and 1 (solid and hazard): it only hurts when Pip bumps it from below. They hang under the floating platform; walk under them, then jump with Z.

Challenge Respawn effect

When Pip respawns, make a ring of particles fly out around it. burst sprays them at random; write a ring function that gives particle i of n the speed vx = math.cos(a), vy = math.sin(a) with a = i / n * 2 * math.pi.

See what it might look like

ring sends 16 white particles out evenly all around Pip when it comes back after losing a life. Fall into the first gap to see it.

Lesson 13 of 20 · 45 minutes

Enemies: walkers and stomping

Add slimes that patrol the ground and turn at walls and ledges. Jump on their heads to squash them; touch them any other way and you get hurt.

In this lesson

  • enemy entities with gravity
  • patrolling and turning at ledges
  • telling a stomp from a side hit
  • bouncing
  • a flattened state that times out

Starting point: lesson12.png · Finished: lesson13.png · Play it

Step 1 Draw the slime

The slime is a blob that squeezes as it slides along. Draw the two frames and the flat one on the SPRITES tab, and the marker on tile 53 (it can look like the slime). Place three slime markers in Green Meadow, each on top of the floor it will walk on: one on the hilltop on screen 2 (column 46, row 10), one on the ground in the tunnel under the big rock on screen 3 (column 71, row 13), and one on the ground before the pit on screen 4 (column 92, row 13).

Check

Run it (CtrlR) and press Z: the slime markers show in the level as tiles that don't move.

Step 2 A walking enemy

New and changed definitions outside the functions (constants, tables, variables): add these to your cart, or replace the old version of the same lines.

Enemies are entities with enemy = true. The slime's box is 6 x 6, smaller than the sprite, so you have to really touch it. Put new_slime above SPAWN, like the other new_ functions.

The slime faces the way it walks: its sprite faces left, so it's flipped when vx > 0.

The slime's update is update_walker. Add an empty one for now, so you can see the slimes first:

Check

Run it and press Z: the slimes sit on the ground where you put the markers, facing left and squeezing in place. Pip walks right through them.

Now replace your empty update_walker with the real one:

The slime uses the same move_x and move_y as Pip, so it falls and collides the same way. It turns around when it walks into a wall, or when it's standing on something and the next step has no floor:

floor_ahead tests the single pixel just past the slime's front edge, one pixel below its feet. Turning at ledges makes slimes stay on their platforms; take that test out and they walk off edges.

update_walker calls touch_enemy. Add an empty one for now:

Check

Run it: the slimes slide back and forth, and each one turns at the edge of its floor. The one before the pit on screen 4 turns at its edge and never falls in. Pip still walks through them. (If the slimes don't move, look for two update_walkers: delete the empty one.)

Step 3 Stomp or ouch?

Every enemy calls touch_enemy when it might touch Pip. Replace your empty touch_enemy with this one:

A stomp is when Pip is falling (vy > 0) and its feet were above the enemy's head on the previous frame: p.y + p.h - p.vy is where Pip's feet were before this frame's move. The + 2 makes stomps a little easier. Anything else is a hit from the side or below.

The squashed slime stays flat for 20 frames, then disappears. Pip bounces up, and higher if the jump button is held: player.jumping lets you cut that bounce short by letting go of the button, like a jump.

Check your work

Slimes slide back and forth and turn at the edges of their floor (the slime before the pit on screen 4 never falls in). Landing on one squashes it (+100) and bounces Pip; walking into one costs a heart.

Challenge Faster slimes

Make slimes speed up for a moment when Pip is close and on the same level, as if they're charging.

See what it might look like

When Pip comes within 48 pixels on the same level, a slime turns toward Pip and slides three times as fast for half a second, then rests for half a second. Walk into the tunnel under the big rock and jump over the slime there as it charges.

Challenge Edge walkers

Make a second kind of slime (draw new sprites in another color: copy 272-274 to free sprite slots and recolor them) that does not turn at ledges and walks off them.

Hint

Give it a field, like careful = false, and only check floor_ahead when e.careful is true.

See what it might look like

Orange slimes (sprites 281-283, marker tile 63) have careful = false, so they skip the ledge test and walk off edges. One starts on the hilltop next to a green slime and walks down the hill, while the green one turns back at the edge.

Challenge Combo

Stomping several enemies without touching the ground gives more points each time: 100, 200, 400… Reset the combo when Pip lands.

See what it might look like

player.combo starts at 100, is added to the score and doubles with each stomp, and landing sets it back to 100. Two more slimes join the one on the hilltop: bounce from one to the next (hold Z for high bounces) and the score goes 100, 300, 700.

+-- == Enemies ==
+-- Every enemy has e.enemy = true. Touching one hurts Pip, unless Pip lands
+-- on its head: that's a stomp.
+function new_slime(x, y)
+  add_ent({
+    x = x + 1, y = y + 2, w = 6,
+    h = 6, vx = -0.4, vy = 0,
+    enemy = true,
+    update = update_walker,
+    draw = draw_slime, squashed = 0
+  })
+end
+
+-- Is there floor just past the front edge of e? (so it can turn at ledges)
+function floor_ahead(e)
+  local fx =
+    e.vx > 0 and e.x + e.w or e.x - 1
+  return box_hits(fx, e.y + e.h, 1, 1)
+end
+
+function update_walker(e)
+  if e.squashed > 0 then          -- flattened: wait a moment, then vanish
+    e.squashed = e.squashed - 1
+    if e.squashed == 0 then
+      e.dead = true
+    end
+    return
+  end
+  e.vy = math.min(e.vy + P.gravity,
+      P.max_fall)
+  if move_y(e, e.vy) then e.vy = 0 end
+  -- walk; turn around at walls, and at ledges when standing on something
+  local on_ground =
+    box_hits(e.x, e.y + 1, e.w, e.h)
+  if move_x(e, e.vx) or (on_ground
+        and not floor_ahead(e)) then
+    e.vx = -e.vx
+  end
+  if e.y > (lvl.y + lvl.h) * 8 then
+    e.dead = true
+  end
+  touch_enemy(e)
+end
+
+-- Pip touches an enemy: stomp it if Pip is falling onto its head.
+function touch_enemy(e)
+  local p = player
+  if not overlaps(p, e) then
+    return
+  end
+  local was_above =
+    p.y + p.h - p.vy <= e.y + 2   -- feet were above its head last frame
+  if p.vy > 0 and was_above then
+    stomp(e)
+  else
+    hurt(e.x + e.w / 2)
+  end
+end
+
+function stomp(e)
+  e.squashed = 20
+  e.vx = 0
+  score = score + 100
+  burst(e.x + 3, e.y + 3, 8, 6)
+  -- bounce off its head; higher if the jump button is held
+  player.vy = btn(BTN_A)
+    and P.jump_speed or -2.5
+  player.jumping = btn(BTN_A)    -- a high bounce can be cut short, like a jump
+end
+
+function draw_slime(e)
+  local id =
+    e.squashed > 0 and SPR_SLIME_FLAT
+    or anim_frame(ANIM_SLIME, 12)
+  spr(id, e.x - 1 - cam.x,
+      e.y - 2 - cam.y, 0, 1,
+      e.vx > 0 and 1 or 0)
+end
+

 -- Lose a heart, unless Pip is still blinking from the last hit.
