Lesson 14 of 20 · 50 minutes

Enemies: flyers, shooters and spikies

Three new enemies, each with its own trick: a swooping bat, a turret that fires bullets and a spiky you must not stomp.

In this lesson

  • movement that follows a curve (math.sin)
  • enemies that create entities
  • projectiles
  • enemies that change the stomp rule

Starting point: lesson13.png · Finished: lesson14.png · Play it

Step 1 Draw the new enemies

Draw them, and their markers on the TILES tab: 54 (bat), 55 (turret), 56 (spiky). Place a bat in the air over the gap just after the big rock on screen 3 (column 82, row 9), a turret on top of the big rock, one cell from its right end (column 76, row 8), and a spiky on the ground at the end of the level, after the last pillar (column 115, row 13).

New and changed definitions outside the functions (constants, tables, variables): add these to your cart, or replace the old version of the same lines.

The new markers go into SPAWN (in the new definitions above). Their new_ functions don't exist yet, so for now those entries are nil and the markers stay tiles.

Check

Run it (CtrlR) and press Z: the three new markers sit in the level as tiles that don't move, and there's no error.

Step 2 The bat: flying on a curve

A bat doesn't fall or walk. It swoops left and right around where it started and bobs up and down. Both come from math.sin, which swings smoothly between -1 and 1. Like every new_ function, new_bat goes above SPAWN:

The left-right swing (32 pixels each way) is slow; the up-down bob (6 pixels) is three times faster, which makes the flight look like flapping. phase comes from the bat's map column, so bats in different places start at different points of the flight and don't move in step. You can still stomp a bat: touch_enemy works for any enemy.

Check

Run it: the bat swoops left and right over the gap after the big rock, bobbing up and down. It turns just past the right end of the rock. Stand on the ground there and jump up into it as it turns over Pip's head: a heart goes. Then climb onto the rock and take a running jump off its right end onto the bat: Pip bounces and gets 100 points, but the bat keeps flying (step 4 fixes that). Keep holding Right as Pip bounces, or it drops into the gap.

Step 3 The turret and its bullets

The turret stands still, and fires bullets when Pip is close: less than 120 pixels away across and 48 up or down. The bullets come first, so the turret has something to fire. A bullet is an entity too: it flies straight and is removed when it hits a wall, runs out of time or hits Pip:

Bullets aren't enemies (no enemy = true): you can't stomp them, and they handle touching Pip themselves.

Check

Run it: nothing makes bullets yet, but there's no error.

Now the turret:

reload counts down; when it reaches zero and Pip is near, the turret creates a new entity, one of your bullets, and starts reloading (90 frames). The turret flips to face Pip:

Check

Run it: the turret on top of the big rock turns to face Pip, and fires when Pip is close. On the ground under the rock, its shots fly over Pip's head. Climb onto the big rock: the turret fires along the top of the rock, at Pip. A bullet that hits Pip costs a heart.

Step 4 The spiky: no stomping

The spiky walks like a slime, so it reuses update_walker. Its back is covered in spikes, so landing on it hurts:

Like the slime, it faces the way it walks:

Check

Run it: the spiky near the end of the level walks and turns like a slime. For now, landing on it still squashes it and makes it vanish.

stomp now checks for a spiky first. And enemies without a flat sprite (the bat, the turret) just disappear when stomped:

Check your work

The bat swoops over the gap after the big rock; stomping it makes it pop (so does the turret). The turret on the big rock turns to face Pip and fires when Pip is close, even when Pip is on the ground under the rock (those shots fly over Pip's head); a bullet costs a heart. Jumping on the spiky hurts Pip instead of the spiky.

Challenge Aimed shots

Make the turret aim at Pip in two dimensions: give bullets a vy too, from the direction to Pip divided by the distance, times the speed.

Hint

local dx, dy = player.x - e.x, player.y - e.y; local d = math.sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy); then vx = dx / d * 1.5, vy = dy / d * 1.5. To see it work, jump up near the turret: its shots aim up at Pip. A shot aimed down at Pip on the ground can hit the big rock under the turret right away.

See what it might look like

Each bullet gets a vx and a vy from the direction to Pip, so the turret on the big rock fires straight at Pip, up and down as well as across. Stand at the other end of the rock and jump: the shots fly up at Pip.

Challenge Dive bomber

Make a new bat that hangs still until Pip walks underneath, then dives straight down.

See what it might look like

The dive bomber (marker tile 61) hangs upside down until Pip is right below it, then drops 3 pixels a frame and bursts on the ground. One hangs under the cloud on screen 1: keep running!

Challenge Defeat the spiky

Spikies can't be stomped, but a bullet could hit them. Make bullets defeat enemies they touch. (Careful: a bullet starts inside its own turret. Pass the turret e from update_turret to new_bullet, keep it in the bullet as owner, and skip that enemy.)

See what it might look like

A bullet that touches an enemy other than its owner (the turret that fired it) removes both. A turret and a spiky were added on screen 1: walk toward them and the turret's shot takes out the spiky first.

+    x = x, y = y, w = 4, h = 4,
+    vx = vx, life = 180,
+    update = update_bullet,
+    draw = draw_bullet
+  })
+end
+
+function update_bullet(e)
+  e.x = e.x + e.vx
+  e.life = e.life - 1
+  if e.life <= 0 or box_hits(e.x, e.y,
+        e.w, e.h) then
+    e.dead = true
+    burst(e.x + 2, e.y + 2, 4, 3)
+  elseif overlaps(player, e) then
+    e.dead = true
+    hurt(e.x)
+  end
+end
+
+function draw_bullet(e)
+  spr(SPR_BULLET, e.x - 2 - cam.x,
+      e.y - 2 - cam.y, 0)

Lesson 15 of 20 · 60 minutes

Sound effects

Make the game's sounds in TIC-80's SFX editor and play them from code at the right moments.

In this lesson

  • how TIC-80 makes sound
  • waveforms
  • volume, arpeggio and pitch envelopes
  • loops and speed
  • sfx() and sound channels
  • an extra life every 50 coins

Starting point: lesson14.png · Finished: lesson15.png · Play it

Step 1 How TIC-80 makes sound

TIC-80 has 4 sound channels: four sounds can play at once. A sound effect (an SFX, 64 of them per cart) is a short recipe of 30 ticks. For each tick it says:

  • which waveform to play (the shape of the sound wave, which decides its color: buzzy, soft, noisy),
  • how loud (0-15),
  • an arpeggio step (how many notes above the base note),
  • a fine pitch change.

At speed 0 a tick lasts one frame, so an SFX is half a second long; faster speeds squeeze it, slower ones stretch it. The SFX also has a base note, which sfx() can change: the same SFX can play high or low.

Step 2 Open the SFX editor

Press F4.

Explore this lesson's finished sounds in the Sound Lab: the real SFX editor, with the sounds listed by name. Click a sound to hear it and watch the ticks play, and point at any part of the editor to find out what it does. Then change a graph and play the sound again: the lab tells you what you changed, Reset puts it back, and Save my sounds gives you a cart with your version.

Step 3 Draw the waveforms

A waveform is 32 samples, each 0 to 15. There are 16 waveform slots, shared by every SFX in the cart. Click a slot button (the 16 small buttons under the wave picture), then draw its samples on the picture with the mouse: each column is a sample, higher is bigger. Pip's Peak uses seven:

WaveShape32 samples (0-f)
0noise (all zeros)00000000000000000000000000000000
1squareffffffffffffffff0000000000000000
2pulse 25%ffffffff000000000000000000000000
3pulse 12.5%ffff0000000000000000000000000000
4triangle02468acefffffffffedcba9876543210
5saw00112233445566778899aabbccddeeff
6sine89acdeefffeedca98653211000112356

Waveform 0 is all zeros: TIC-80 plays an all-zero (or all-15) wave as noise, which is what explosions and drums need.

Square and pulse waves are bright and buzzy (classic game music); a triangle is soft and round (good for bass); a sine is the softest. The narrower the pulse, the thinner the sound.

Clicking a slot button also sets all 30 ticks of the SFX you're editing to that wave. That's handy when a sound uses one wave all the way through (most do), but it means you should draw the waveforms first, while you're on an SFX you haven't made yet.

Step 4 How to read the tables

Each sound below comes with a table. A row of numbers is one value per tick, from tick 0: draw them from left to right, one column per tick. A row that ends in … keeps its last value to the end (tick 29): draw that too, because nothing fills in the rest for you. The rows:

  • WAV: the waveform slot of each tick. If it's one number, just click that slot button.
  • VOL: the loudness of each tick, 0 (silent) to 15. In the graph, loudness n is a bar n + 1 lights tall: 15 fills the column, 0 is a single light. Hover over the graph to see the value. A new SFX starts at full volume on every tick, so a sound that should end must have its last ticks drawn down to 0.
  • ARPEGG: how many notes to add on top of the SFX's note, per tick (0 to 15). DOWN on means they go downward instead.
  • PITCH: a fine pitch change per tick, -8 to 7 (the middle line is 0). x16 on makes it 16 times stronger.
  • SPD: the speed, and how many of the 8 little bars to light.
  • Note: the key to click on the piano.
  • LOOP: the part of a graph that repeats while the note is held (most sounds have none).

Step 5 Make the jump sound

  1. Select SFX 0: click the top-left square of the SFX grid (at the top left of the editor). Left and Right step to the other SFX; IDX shows the number.
  2. Click waveform slot 2: every tick now uses wave 2.
  3. The top graph shows VOL at first. Draw the volume from the table: loud at the start, down to 0 (a single light) at tick 14, and a single light in every column after that. Hold Shift while dragging to draw a flat line.
  4. In the ARPEGG graph, draw a ramp from 0 up to 12: the note climbs an octave as the sound plays.
  5. Click the sixth of the 8 little bars next to SPD, so 6 are lit: speed 1, a quick sound.
  6. On the piano at the bottom, click A in the fifth octave from the left (A-5): that's the SFX's own note. Clicking a key also plays the sound.

To hear it again, hold Space (the sound stops when you let go). The note keys (Z S X…, like a piano) play it too, but careful: they also change the SFX's note. Click A-5 again afterwards.

Step 6 The other sounds

Listen to them, then build them in SFX 1-14 from the tables.

Two of them (3 and 12) use a LOOP: under each graph, the LOOP row has two numbers with little arrows, the loop's start tick and its size (in hex, 0-F, where A-F mean 10-15; size 0 means no loop). While the sound plays, the looped ticks repeat, which keeps a buzz or a trill going.

SFX 6 (spring), 8 (boss hit) and 9 (explosion) are used in later lessons; you can make them now or then:

Step 7 Play sounds from code

sfx(id, note, duration, channel) starts an SFX. The music (next lesson) uses channels 0-2, so sounds always go on channel 3:

New and changed definitions outside the functions (constants, tables, variables): add these to your cart, or replace the old version of the same lines.

Leaving out note (or passing nil) plays the SFX at the note you set in the editor, but passing -1 does not; it plays the lowest note there is. That's why play passes nil. A duration of -1 lets the sound play to its end.

Check

Run it (CtrlR): nothing changes yet, but there's no error.

Now call play where things happen. When a jump starts:

Check

Run it and jump: the rising jump sound plays every time Pip leaves the ground. No sound? Check SFX 0 in the SFX editor (Space plays it).

The others, each one line in a function you already have:

FunctionWhereLine
update_pickupwhen a gem is takenplay(SND.GEM)
update_checkpointwhen the flag goes upplay(SND.CHECKPOINT)
stompafter the burstplay(SND.STOMP)
update_turretwhen a bullet is firedplay(SND.SHOOT)
hurtat the endplay(SND.HURT)

Check

Run it: press Z on the title screen (the menu sound), then stomp a slime, get hit, touch a checkpoint flag, take a gem and fall in a pit. Each has its own sound. Coins are still silent.

Step 8 An extra life every 50 coins

Coins get their sound from add_coins, which gives a life every 50 coins and plays the 1-up jingle instead of the coin sound:

Now update_pickup calls it instead of adding to coins directly:

Check your work

Every action has a sound: jumping rises, coins ding, stomps thump, hurting buzzes. Sounds never pile up into a mess: they all share channel 3, so a new sound replaces the one playing. Every 50th coin plays the 1-up jingle and adds a life. To try it without collecting 50 coins, start the game with 49 coins: in update_title, change the second 0 in 0, 0, 0, START_LIVES to 49. Put it back to 0 afterwards.

Challenge A landing sound

Make a soft, short noise SFX and play it when Pip lands from a fast fall (where the squash starts).

See what it might look like

Instead of a new SFX, this example borrows SFX 7 (the shoot noise) and plays it at a low note (36) and volume 6 (sfx's fifth argument) where the squash starts. Jump with Z and listen as Pip lands; with your own soft noise in a free slot, play it there instead.

Challenge Pitch with height

Play the coin sound at a higher note for coins collected higher up: pass a note to sfx instead of nil, for example sfx(SND.COIN, 72 + (lvl.y * 8 + 136 - e.y) // 16, -1, 3). Notes are numbers: 12 per octave, starting from C-1 at 0, so 72 is C-7, just above the coin's own note (B-6). Use //, not /: sfx stops the game with an error if the note isn't a whole number.

See what it might look like

play and add_coins take a note, and each coin passes one from its height: the coins on the ground ding at note 73, the row over the floating platform at 75. Collect coins at different heights and listen.

Challenge Your own sound

Replace the jump sound with your own. Try the saw wave, a falling arpeggio, or a slower speed. Which feels best?

Lesson 16 of 20 · 60 minutes

Music

Write the game's music in TIC-80's tracker (patterns of notes played by instrument SFX, arranged into tracks). Then play the right track in each part of the game.

In this lesson

  • trackers: rows, patterns, frames and tracks
  • instruments made from SFX
  • entering notes with the keyboard
  • tempo and speed
  • music()
  • music for each game state

Starting point: lesson15.png · Finished: lesson16.png · Play it

Step 1 How the tracker works

TIC-80's music editor is a tracker. Time runs down the screen in rows; at the default tempo, 10 rows play per second.

  • A pattern is 64 rows of one channel: a melody, a bass line, a drum beat. Each row can start a note.
  • A frame says which pattern each of the 4 channels plays at the same time.
  • A track is a list of frames played in order: a whole song. A cart has 8 tracks, music(0) to music(7).

Each note is played by an SFX: the SFX is the instrument. So you make instruments in the SFX editor first.

Press F5. The music editor opens in piano mode (notes as a grid you click). This course uses tracker mode, where you type notes: click the TRACKER MODE button, the right-most icon at the top right.

Explore the course's music in the Sound Lab: the real music editor, already in tracker mode, with the songs listed by name. Click a song to play it and watch the rows go by; mute a channel, or solo one, to hear each part on its own. Then change a note's octave or the TEMPO and play it again: the lab lists what you changed, and Reset brings the original back.

Step 2 Make the instruments

Instruments are ordinary SFX, made in the SFX editor like your sound effects. The melody, bass and pad instruments keep their volume up, so a note lasts until the next note (or a note-off) in its channel; the drums and the bell fade out on their own. Make SFX 16-23 with these settings:

The kick drum is a square wave whose arpeggio falls fast (that falling pitch is what makes a thump); the snare and hi-hat are noise, short and shorter.

Step 3 Set up a track

In tracker mode:

  1. TRACK: click its right arrow until it shows 01.
  2. TEMPO, SPD and ROWS: set them to the values in the track's table below (track 1: 150, 6, 64). Click the arrows beside a value, or left-click the value to raise it by one and right-click to lower it (Shift+click: by ten), or drag sideways.
  3. Click frame 00 in the list on the left.
  4. Above each of the four channels is a box with a pattern number: the pattern that channel plays in this frame. Click a box (it turns red), type two digits, for example 01, and press Enter to go back to the notes. (Clicking the red box again adds one.) 00 means the channel is silent in this frame, and you can't type notes into it.

Step 4 Enter notes

Click a row in a channel to put the cursor there. Then:

  • The bottom two rows of letters play notes, like a piano: Z is C, S C#, X D, D D#, C E, V F, G F#, B G, H G#, N A, J A#, M B. The row above (Q 2 W …) is one octave higher. The cursor moves down a row after each note.
  • A new note gets the octave and the SFX (instrument) of the last note you typed. To change them, move the cursor onto a note's octave digit and type a new one (1-8), or onto its two SFX digits and type the SFX number; the notes you type after that use the new values. Shift+Z and Shift+X also move the octave down and up.
  • A enters a note-off (the note stops). Delete empties a row, Backspace removes it and pulls the rest up. The arrow keys move the cursor and Tab jumps to the next channel.
  • Space plays the track from the start, Enter plays the current frame; press again to stop. CtrlZ undoes.

Step 5 Write the overworld theme

Track 1 is the music for Green Meadow (and later the Sky Tower). It has two frames, each with a melody (channel 1), a bass line (channel 2) and drums (channel 3). Channel 4 stays empty on purpose: the sound effects play there. Listen to it, then look at it in the tracker: each picture is one whole frame, all 64 rows from top to bottom (the editor shows 16 rows at a time; scroll down to see the rest).

In each column, a note shows its name and octave (E-6), then its SFX in orange (16, the lead instrument). Rows with dashes are empty: the note before keeps playing. A note-off (== below) shows no note, just the dashes on the right.

To copy the notes exactly, here are the same patterns as text. Each item is one row, . means an empty row, == is a note-off, and a note like E-6 uses the instrument in the pattern's header line. C-4:18 means C-4 played with SFX 18: in the drums pattern every hit says which drum it is.

Step 6 The other tracks

Listen to the other tracks:

You can type them in from the notes below, or copy them from the lesson cart: load lesson16.png sfx copies the SFX and waveforms into your cart and load lesson16.png music the patterns and tracks. Then save (see Loading a lesson cart).

The notes of every other track

A track plays its frames in order and loops back to frame 0 after the last one that has patterns in it. Short jingles that shouldn't loop are played with loop set to false, below. The rows setting at the top makes a frame shorter than 64 rows: the jingles use 32.

Step 7 Play music in each state

Each level says which track it uses:

Check

Run it (CtrlR): nothing changes yet, but there's no error. (A missing comma after sky = 10 shows up here.)

Change the music in set_state:

music(track) starts a track and loops it; music() with no arguments stops the music. music(MUS.GAME_OVER, -1, -1, false) plays from the start (frame -1 and row -1 mean "the default") without looping.

Check

Run it: the title screen is still silent. Press Z: the overworld theme starts. Fall in a pit: the music stops, and starts again when Pip comes back.

The title screen is the first state, but set_state("title") is never called at the very start, so BOOT starts the title music:

Check your work

The title screen plays the gentle title theme; starting the game switches to the overworld theme. Losing a life stops the music; respawning starts it again. Game over plays a short sad jingle once. Sound effects play on top of the music without cutting it off. A track you haven't made plays nothing: the title music needs track 0, and game over needs track 5.

Challenge A faster theme on the last heart

music takes a tempo after the loop and sustain arguments: music(track, frame, row, loop, sustain, tempo). Play the overworld theme faster (tempo 180) while Pip has one heart left.

See what it might look like

When Pip is down to one heart, the overworld theme starts again at tempo 180; respawning brings back the normal tempo. Run into a slime twice to hear it.

Challenge Your own theme

Write a new melody for the meadow, on top of the existing bass and drums. Keep it in C major: use only the notes C D E F G A B.

Challenge A star theme

Make a short, fast, looping track for later (lesson 17's star power-up): a quick arpeggio over a pulsing bass.

See what it might look like

Track 7: a C-F-G-F arpeggio, one note per row at tempo 200, over a bass that jumps between root and octave. You type it into the tracker; the example's title screen plays it so you can hear it.

Lesson 17 of 20 · 60 minutes

Power-ups

Add ?-blocks that Pip opens by jumping into them from below, and four power-ups that come out of them: a heart, a feather for a double jump, speed boots and a star, which makes Pip flash through colors with the palette map.

In this lesson

  • blocks that react when hit from below
  • changing the map while the game runs with mset
  • items that pop out of blocks
  • timed and permanent power-ups
  • a double jump
  • the palette map (poke4 at 0x3FF0)

Starting point: lesson16.png · Finished: lesson17.png · Play it

Step 1 Draw the blocks and the items

All five ?-blocks can look the same (the player isn't supposed to know what's inside), or you can give each a small hint. The used block (21) is the plain, dark version.

Then set the sprite flags. On the TILES tab, for tiles 16 to 21, turn on flag 0 (solid): Pip can stand on blocks. For tiles 16 to 20 (not 21), also turn on flag 4: in this game flag 4 means bonus block.

Step 2 Put blocks in the levels

In the map editor, on screen 2 of Green Meadow, place three blocks in a row in the air over the hilltop (row 7, columns 44-46): tiles 16 20 16, a coin block, a star block and another coin block. Pip bumps them by jumping from the hilltop. Near the end of the meadow, over the flat ground before the three pillars, put a heart block (17) at column 87, row 10 (the right end of screen 3), and a feather block (18) at column 91, row 10 (the start of screen 4). Row 10 is low enough to bump from the ground, and high enough to walk under. The boots block (19) is for the Crystal Cave, which you'll build in the next lesson.

Check

Run it (CtrlR) and press Z: three blocks float over the hilltop. They're solid: jump into them from the hilltop and Pip bonks its head. To check the flags, press Esc until you see the console: eval trace(fget(16, 4)) prints true, and eval trace(fget(21, 4)) prints false.

Because the tile id says what is inside, the code doesn't need a list of blocks:

New and changed definitions outside the functions (constants, tables, variables): add these to your cart, or replace the old version of the same lines.

Check

Run it: nothing changes yet, but there's no error.

Step 3 Hitting a block from below

move_y already stops Pip when its head hits something. Now, when that happens on the way up, update_player calls bump_head:

bump_head looks at the tiles just above Pip's head, one for each column Pip covers (Pip's box can be across two tiles), and opens every one that has flag 4.

mset(x, y, tile) changes the map while the game runs: the ?-block becomes a used block, which has flag 0 but not flag 4, so it stays solid and can't be opened again. A coin block gives its coin right away; the other blocks make an item.

mset changes the map in RAM, not in the cart. That's why load_level starts with sync(4, 0, false) (lesson 10): it copies the map back from the cart, so every new game starts with fresh ?-blocks.

Check

Run it, go to the hilltop, stand still under the left end of the left block (a coin block) and jump into it: it turns dark, the bump sound plays, sparkles fly out and the coin count goes up. Leave the star block in the middle, and the heart and feather blocks, for now: their items come next, and hitting one now stops the game with an error about new_item. Pip is narrow, but if it's under two blocks when it jumps, it opens both.

Step 4 Items

An item is one more kind of entity. It rises out of its block (half a pixel per frame, until it's 7 pixels higher), then slides away from Pip, drops off its block like a walker and waits on the ground, bobbing.

ITEM_SPRITE[e.kind] turns the block's tile id into the item's sprite.

Check

Run it and go to the heart block, over the flat ground before the three pillars at the end of the meadow. Jump into it: a heart rises out, slides off the block, drops to the ground and bobs. Don't walk into it yet: taking it needs power_up, next (the game stops with an error naming it).

Step 5 The power-ups

Check

Run it: let an enemy hit Pip once, then take the heart: a sparkle, the power-up sound, and the lost heart is back.

Each power-up is a field in player:

FieldPower-upHow long
hpheart: one heart back
feathera second jump in the airuntil Pip gets hurt, or the level ends
bootsrun 1.5 times faster600 frames (10 s), counts down
starcan't be hurt; enemies touched are defeated480 frames (8 s), counts down

Add them to player (in the new definitions above) and reset them in reset_player, which runs at every level start and respawn:

Count the timers down at the end of update_player:

The boots change the run speed:

Check

The boots block goes in the Crystal Cave next lesson, so give Pip the boots from the console. Run it and press Z to start, then press Esc until you see the console and type eval power_up(19) (19 is the boots block's tile). Type resume to go back to the game: Pip runs faster for 10 seconds, then normal again.

Step 6 The double jump

The feather gives Pip one jump in the air. air_jump says whether that jump is still available: landing gives it back (if Pip has the feather), and using it takes it away.

A normal jump needs coyote > 0 (Pip is on the ground or just left it). If coyote is 0, Pip is in the air, so this jump must be the feather's.

Pip loses the feather when it gets hurt:

Check

Run it and hit the feather block (column 91, next to the heart block), then take the feather: press Z in the air and Pip jumps again, once per jump. Get hit, and the extra jump is gone.

Step 7 A gem for the feather

A power-up is more fun when the level gives it a job. Near the end of Green Meadow, a gem floats over the gap between the last two pillars, at column 107, row 6: one jump from the middle pillar reaches it. Move it two cells up, out of reach of a single jump. In the map editor, middle-click the gem to pick up its tile (49) and click column 107, row 4 to put it there. Then pick the empty tile (0, the top-left of the sheet) and click row 6 to clear the old one.

Now that gem asks for the feather: jump from the middle pillar, and press Z again at the top of the jump.

Step 8 The star

While the star lasts, hurt returns right away (see p.star > 0 above), and any enemy Pip touches is defeated:

The star also makes Pip flash through colors. Instead of drawing more sprites for that, you can use the palette map.

Step 9 The palette map

When TIC-80 draws a pixel of color c, it first looks c up in a 16-entry table, the palette map, at RAM address 0x3FF0, and draws the color it finds there. Normally entry c holds c, so nothing changes. Change entry 6 to 2 and everything drawn in green (color 6) comes out red (color 2) instead, until you change it back.

Each entry is 4 bits (half a byte, a nibble). poke4(address, value) writes one nibble; nibble addresses are byte addresses times 2. So entry i of the palette map is nibble 0x3FF0 * 2 + i:

2 + t // 4 % 4 cycles through colors 2, 3, 4 and 5 (red, orange, yellow, light green), changing every 4 frames. The map is changed only while spr draws Pip, and put back right after, so nothing else changes color.

The palette map changes what's drawn; the palette (0x3FC0, lesson 4) changes what each color looks like on the screen. With the map you swap colors of some sprites; with the palette you change the whole screen at once.

Check

Run it and take the star: Pip flashes red, orange, yellow and green, and any slime it touches is knocked out. After 8 seconds Pip is green again and enemies hurt again.

Step 10 Show the power-ups in the HUD

The HUD shows an icon for each power-up Pip has, with the seconds left for the timed ones:

(player.boots + 59) // 60 turns frames into whole seconds, rounding up: 600 and 599 frames are both 10 s, 1 frame is 1 s.

Check your work

Jumping into a ?-block from below turns it dark and plays the bump sound; the coin blocks give a coin, the others release an item that rises, slides off its block and waits on the ground. The heart gives a heart back (never more than three). With the feather, Pip can jump once more in the air, until hurt. The star makes Pip flash and defeat enemies for 8 seconds. The HUD shows what Pip has, and the star's icon counts down the seconds. The boots get their block in the next lesson; to see their icon count down now, use eval power_up(19) and resume again, as in step 5.

Challenge Brick blocks

Make a breakable brick tile: jumping into it from below turns it into empty space (mset(tx, ty, 0)) with a burst of orange particles (color 3). Give it its own flag.

Hint

Add a flag, like F_BRICK = 5, and in bump_head check it next to F_BONUS.

See what it might look like

Tile 35 is a brick with flags 0 (solid) and 5 (brick): bump it from below and it breaks into orange-brown bits. There are four bricks just right of the start; jump under them with Z.

Challenge A multi-coin block

Make a block that gives a coin every time it's hit, up to 5 times, before turning into a used block. Keep the counts in a table with keys like string.format("%d,%d", tx, ty). (tx and ty can be numbers like 9.0, which .. would turn into the text "9.0", so format them as whole numbers.)

See what it might look like

Tile 35 looks like any ?-block (flags 0 and 4), but it gives a coin on each of its first five hits; block_hits counts them by "tx,ty". Jump under the block just right of the start with Z again and again.

Challenge Star music

Use the star track you wrote in lesson 16's challenge: play it while the star lasts, and go back to the level's music when it ends.

See what it might look like

Grabbing a star plays track 7, the star theme from lesson 16's challenge (BOOT writes it into music RAM here); when the star runs out, the level's music comes back. There's a star block right of the start: jump under it with Z, then catch the star.

+function bump_head(p)

+end
+
+-- An item slides up out of its block, then waits to be picked up.
+function new_item(x, y, kind)
+  add_ent({
+    x = x + 1, y = y, w = 6, h = 6,
+    top = y - 7, kind = kind, vx = 0,
+    vy = 0, rising = true,
+    landed = false,
+    update = update_item,
+    draw = draw_item

+end
+
+function update_item(e)
+  if e.rising then
+    e.y = e.y - 0.5
+    if e.y <= e.top then          -- out of the block: slide away from Pip
+      e.rising = false
+      e.vx = player.x < e.x and 0.75
+        or -0.75
+    end
+  elseif not e.landed then
+    -- slide off the block and drop to the ground, like a walker
+    if move_x(e, e.vx) then
+      e.vx = -e.vx
+    end
+    e.vy = math.min(e.vy + P.gravity,
+        P.max_fall)
+    if move_y(e, e.vy) then
+      -- down off the blocks and onto something: stay there
+      if e.y > e.top + 4 then
+        e.landed = true
+      end
+      e.vy = 0
+    end
+  end
+  if not e.rising
+      and overlaps(player, e) then
+    e.dead = true
+    power_up(e.kind)
+  end
+end
+
+function draw_item(e)
+  local bob = e.landed and (

+  spr(ITEM_SPRITE[e.kind],
+      e.x - 1 - cam.x,

+  end

+end

Lesson 18 of 20 · 90 minutes

New worlds

Two new levels, the Crystal Cave and the Sky Tower, with platforms you can jump up through, slippery ice, bubbling lava, springs and moving platforms, and a goal flag that takes Pip to the next level.

In this lesson

  • one-way platforms and dropping through them
  • tiles with special physics (ice)
  • animating tiles with map()'s remap function
  • springs
  • moving platforms that carry the player
  • a goal and a level-clear state
  • several levels in one map

Starting point: lesson17.png · Finished: lesson18.png · Play it

Step 1 Draw the new tiles and gadgets

The cave needs rock, a dark wall to put behind everything, crystals, lava for the top of a pool (two frames) and deep lava for under it:

The Sky Tower is built from bricks, with two kinds of one-way platform (a wooden plank for the cave, a cloud for the sky) and an ice block:

And the gadgets: a spring (squeezed and relaxed), a piece of moving platform, the goal flag, and their markers:

The Map Lab has this lesson's whole map. Jump to each level, and point at a cell to see what it is: a marker, like a coin or a spring, says what the level loader turns it into.

Step 4 One-way platforms

A one-way platform stops Pip only when Pip falls onto its top edge. Jumping up through it, or walking through it sideways, does nothing.

The idea: before moving, remember where Pip's feet were (old_bottom). math.ceil(old_bottom / 8) * 8 is the first tile edge at or below the old feet. If the new feet went past that edge, and the row of pixels along the edge touches a one-way tile, Pip's feet crossed the platform's top this frame: land on it. A Pip that started below the top (jumping up through it) never crosses it going down, so it passes through.

box_hits (flag 0) still decides the ordinary walls, so it knows nothing about one-way tiles. Standing still on one is checked separately:

Pip uses it now: in update_player, p.ground = on_ground(p) replaces the box_hits line.

Check

Run it: jump up through the plank near the start, and Pip lands on top. Jump again from there. Walk off the end and Pip falls.

Slimes use on_ground too. In update_walker, delete the local on_ground = lines and start the if with:

and floor_ahead treats a one-way platform as floor too, so slimes patrol on them:

Check

Run it and walk right to the lava: up on the high shelf, the slime still walks back and forth. If you get "attempt to call a boolean value (local 'on_ground')", the old local on_ground = lines are still in update_walker: delete them.

Dropping through

Holding Down and pressing jump on a one-way platform drops Pip through it:

not box_hits(...) makes sure Pip is standing on a one-way platform, not on solid ground. p.drop counts down 10 frames, and while it's above 0, move_y and on_ground ignore one-way platforms, so Pip falls through. (BTN_DOWN is one of the new constants above.)

player has two new fields, drop and ride (for the moving platforms, later). reset_player sets them back when Pip starts again: add this line at its end:

Check

Run it: stand on the plank, hold Down and press Z. Pip drops through to the floor.

Step 5 Bubbling lava with remap

Lava should move. Instead of changing the map with mset every few frames, give map() a remap function as its last argument. For every cell it draws, map() calls remap(tile, x, y) and draws the tile the function returns instead. The map itself never changes.

(t // 16 + x) % 2 swaps the two lava frames every 16 frames, and neighboring cells (+ x) are always on opposite frames, so the lava looks like it's churning. Pass the function to map in draw_play:

The arguments before it: 0 is the transparent color and 1 the scale.

Check

Run it: the lava next to the start bubbles.

Step 6 Moving platforms

A moving platform is three platform sprites wide (24 pixels). It slides along a sine wave: 40 pixels each way for a left-right platform (dx = 1), 24 for an up-down one (dy = 1).

Put these functions above SPAWN, and add the two platform markers to it, after [M_SPIKY]:

Check

Run it: next to the high shelf, a platform glides up and down. Don't count on it yet: jump onto it, and Pip falls right through.

The tricky part is carrying Pip. Each frame, after Pip moves, land_on_platforms checks whether Pip's feet came down onto a platform's top, and if so, puts Pip on it and remembers it in p.ride. The next frame, update_platform moves its rider by the same amount it moved itself, so Pip goes along.

The math.max(0, -(e.my or 0)) gives some extra leeway when the platform is moving up, since it rises into Pip's feet. update_player remembers where Pip's feet were before the vertical move, and calls it right after on_ground:

Check

Run it: jump onto the platform when it comes down, and it carries Pip up. Hold Right, and Pip steps off onto the high shelf when the platform gets there. Past the shelf, the next platform carries Pip over the lava lake and back.

Step 7 Ice

On ice, Pip speeds up and slows down much more slowly: P.ice (0.03) replaces both the acceleration and the friction.

box_touches(p.x, p.y + p.h, p.w, 1, F_ICE) looks at the one row of pixels just under Pip's feet.

The ice is in the Sky Tower, so start there for now: change the load_level(2) in update_title to

Check

Run it: the Sky Tower, with Pip at the bottom. The blue ice is up high, out of reach for now.

Step 8 Springs

The spring uses SFX 6 from lesson 15's table: make it now if you skipped it.

A spring is an entity. Touching it from above, or walking into it, launches Pip high (P.spring is -6.5, compared to -4 for a jump). Put all three functions above SPAWN, and add its marker to SPAWN:

p.jumping = false makes the launch full height even if the jump button isn't held, and p.air_jump = p.feather gives back the feather's jump.

Check

Run it: walk right into the spring. Pip shoots up almost three times as high as a jump, onto the cloud above it. From there, jump right onto the blue ice, run, and let go: Pip keeps sliding. If the spring's marker still shows, your spring functions are below SPAWN: move them above it.

Step 9 The goal

The goal flag is two tiles tall. spr has two more arguments after rotate: w and h, the size in sprites. With w = 1, h = 2, it draws sprite 299 and, under it, sprite 315 (the one below 299 on the sheet, which has 16 sprites per row). That's why new_goal moves the box up by 8 pixels and makes it 16 tall.

Every level needs a goal marker: in Green Meadow at column 117, row 13 (the end of screen 4); the Crystal Cave's is at (117, 26), at the top of the steps at its end, and the Sky Tower's at (144, 2), on the peak at the top.

Step 10 Level clear, and winning

Touching the goal starts a new state, "clear". It shows a box with the coins and gems, gives a 1000-point bonus, plays the level-clear jingle, and after 200 frames loads the next level, or, after the last one, goes to the "win" state:

TIC gets two more branches. The "win" one calls update_win and draw_win, which come last; that's safe, because Pip only wins after the Sky Tower.

Check

Run it and touch the flag: the LEVEL CLEAR box, +1000 on the score, and a few seconds later the Crystal Cave starts.

set_state plays the jingles once (loop false):

The cave uses its own track, MUS.CAVE (track 2), set in its LEVELS entry.

Check

Run it and touch the flag: the level-clear jingle plays (track 4), then the cave's music (track 2).

Last, the "win" state, after the Sky Tower: "YOU REACHED THE TOP!", and Z goes back to the title.

Check your work

Pip jumps up through planks and clouds and lands on them; Down + Z drops through. Ice is slippery. The lava bubbles and hurts. Springs launch Pip high; moving platforms carry Pip along. The goal flag shows the level-clear box, then the next level starts: the cave, then the Sky Tower. After the Sky Tower: "YOU REACHED THE TOP!".

Challenge Crumbling platforms

Make a platform that falls away once Pip has stood on it for half a second (30 frames): a marker that spawns an entity, like the moving platform, that starts falling (vy grows) when its counter of frames with Pip on it reaches 30.

See what it might look like

Marker 61 spawns a crumbling platform (sprite 304). It shakes while Pip stands on it, and after 30 frames it falls. Green Meadow's first gap now has a bridge of two pieces: stop on one, then jump off with Z before it drops. Each piece counts its own frames, so the other one stays.

Challenge Conveyor belts

Make a tile that moves Pip along while standing on it: give it a new flag and, in update_player, call move_x(p, 0.5) when Pip stands on one.

See what it might look like

Tile 35 is a conveyor belt with flags 0 (solid) and 5 (conveyor): standing on it moves Pip 0.5 pixels right every frame, on top of its own running. Walk onto the belt right of the start and let go.

+-- == Springs, platforms and the goal ==
+function new_spring(x, y)
+  add_ent({
+    x = x, y = y + 4, w = 8, h = 4,
+    squeeze = 0,
+    update = update_spring,
+    draw = draw_spring
+  })
+end
+
+function update_spring(e)
+  e.squeeze =
+    math.max(0, e.squeeze - 1)
+  local p = player
+  -- walking into it or landing on it both launch Pip
+  if overlaps(p, e) and (p.ground
+        or (p.vy > 0 and p.y + p.h
+          - p.vy <= e.y + 2)) then
+    p.vy = P.spring
+    p.jumping = false              -- a spring launch is not cut short
+    p.air_jump = p.feather
+    e.squeeze = 10
+    play(SND.SPRING)
+  end
+end
+
+function draw_spring(e)
+  spr(e.squeeze > 0
+      and SPR_SPRING_DOWN
+      or SPR_SPRING_UP, e.x - cam.x,
+      e.y - 4 - cam.y, 0)
+end
+
+-- A moving platform glides back and forth (dx = 1) or up and down (dy = 1)
+-- and carries whoever stands on it.
+function new_platform(x, y, dx, dy)
+  add_ent({
+    x = x - 8, y = y + 4, w = 24,
+    h = 4, home_x = x - 8,
+    home_y = y + 4, dx = dx, dy = dy,
+    platform = true,
+    update = update_platform,
+    draw = draw_platform
+  })
+end
+
+function update_platform(e)
+  local a = t / 90
+  local nx =
+    e.home_x + math.sin(a) * 40 * e.dx
+  local ny =
+    e.home_y + math.sin(a) * 24 * e.dy
+  local mx, my = nx - e.x, ny - e.y
+  e.x, e.y = nx, ny
+  if player.ride == e then          -- carry Pip along
+    move_x(player, mx)
+    player.y = e.y - player.h
+  end
+  e.mx, e.my = mx, my
+end
+
+function draw_platform(e)
+  for i = 0, 2 do
+    spr(SPR_PLATFORM, e.x + i * 8
+        - cam.x, e.y - cam.y, 0)
+  end
+end
+
+-- Land on a moving platform if Pip falls onto one this frame.
+function land_on_platforms(p,
+      old_bottom)
+  p.ride = nil
+  if p.vy < 0 then return end
+  for _, e in ipairs(ents) do
+    if e.platform and p.x + p.w > e.x
+      and p.x < e.x + e.w
+       and old_bottom <= e.y + 1
+         + math.max(0, -(e.my or 0))
+         and p.y + p.h >= e.y then
+      p.y, p.vy, p.ground, p.ride =
+        e.y - p.h, 0, true, e
+    end
+  end
+end
+

+    draw = draw_goal
+  })
+end

Lesson 19 of 20 · 75 minutes

The boss: King Glob

A final level with a boss fight, a big 16x16 enemy that hops at Pip, shakes the screen when it lands and can only be hurt while it's dizzy. It has a health bar, gets angrier as it loses, and explodes at the end.

In this lesson

  • big sprites made of 2x2 sprites
  • a state machine for enemy behavior
  • attack patterns and a weak moment
  • a health bar
  • difficulty that rises during the fight
  • screen shake

Starting point: lesson18.png · Finished: lesson19.png · Play it

Step 1 Draw King Glob

King Glob is 16 x 16 pixels: four sprites in a square. In the sprite editor, draw him across sprites 320, 321 (top) and 336, 337 (bottom): those four are a square on the sprite sheet, because each sheet row has 16 sprites.

The sprite editor can edit a 16 x 16 block at once: the canvas zoom slider at the right end of the toolbar sets the canvas to 1 x 1, 2 x 2, 4 x 4 or 8 x 8 sprites. Select sprite 320 with the 2 x 2 size and the canvas shows all four.

The squished frame is for when he lands or is about to jump; the hurt frame (red) for when he's hit.

The throne room has castle tiles and a marker for the boss:

Step 2 The throne room

The throne room is one screen, 30 x 17 cells at map cell (0, 34), below the cave. Give tile 23 flag 0.

New and changed definitions outside the functions (constants, tables, variables): add these to your cart, or replace the old version of the same lines.

Track 3 is the boss music. And there's no goal: the level ends when King Glob is defeated.

To try the throne room without playing through three levels first, make NEW GAME start there for now. In update_title, change load_level(1) to:

You'll put it back at the end of the lesson.

Check

Run it (CtrlR) and press Z: NEW GAME goes straight to the throne room. Its name shows, the boss music plays and Pip can jump onto the planks. King Glob's marker still sits on the right: he comes alive once new_boss exists.

Step 3 Drawing a 2x2 sprite

You met spr's w and h with the goal flag. With w = 2, h = 2, spr(320, x, y, 0, 1, 0, 0, 2, 2) draws 320 and 321 on top and 336 and 337 below them: a 16 x 16 picture.

His sprites and his hit points go with the constants at the top:

He turns to face Pip (flip), and when he's dizzy, three little stars (the HUD star sprite) circle his head.

Step 4 A boss is a state machine

A boss is an entity, but with a mode that says what it's doing, and a timer for how long. Each mode does its own thing and switches to the next mode when the time comes:

ModeWhat happensNext
waitsits still; squishes for the last 15 frames before jumping (a warning)hop when the timer runs out
hopjumps toward Pip, falls with gravity, bounces off wallsdizzy on landing (shakes the screen)
dizzystars circle his head: the only time a stomp hurts himwait when the timer runs out
dyingexplodes for 2 secondsthe win state

Check

Run it: nothing changes yet, but there's no error. Nothing calls draw_boss until King Glob is an entity.

new_boss keeps the boss in a global, boss, so the health bar can find it. (add_ent returns the entity it added.) Like the other new_ functions, it goes above SPAWN, where [M_BOSS] = new_boss (in the new definitions above) spawns him.

At the end, touching King Glob from above always bounces Pip off, but only hurts him while he's dizzy; touching him any other way hurts Pip, except while he's dizzy (then he's harmless). The bounce first puts Pip on top of his head: Pip may have fallen a few pixels into him, and if it were still inside him on the way up, the next frame would count that as a touch from below and hurt Pip. While he's dying, touching him does nothing.

Getting angrier

angry is true when he has half his health or less. Then everything gets harder: he jumps higher and faster, rests less, and every landing calls in two slimes.

Step 5 Hitting the boss

King Glob's sounds are SFX 8 (hit) and 9 (explosion) from lesson 15's table: make them now if you skipped them.

flash shows the hurt frame for 30 frames. After the sixth hit, he goes into dying: every 8 frames, a burst of particles somewhere on him and an explosion sound; then the win state.

Check

Run it: King Glob sits, squishes, then hops toward Pip and lands; stars circle his head while he's dizzy. Touching his side hurts Pip, unless he's dizzy. Stomp him while he's dizzy: he flashes red and the score goes up 500. Six stomps and he explodes, and the old "YOU REACHED THE TOP!" screen appears (you'll change it at the end).

Step 6 The health bar

The red bar is 100 * boss.hp // BOSS_HP pixels wide: the full 100 at 6 hit points, 50 at 3. Call draw_boss_bar() in draw_play, right after draw_hud().

The throne room has no gems, so the HUD hides the gem counter there. In draw_hud:

Check

Run it: "KING GLOB" and a red bar at the top, and no gem counter. Each stomp shortens the bar by a sixth.

Step 7 Screen shake

The screen shakes when King Glob lands or is stomped. shake counts frames; while it's above 0, update_camera nudges the camera by a random amount:

Because everything is drawn relative to the camera, the whole level shakes, but the HUD (drawn without the camera) stays still.

Check

Run it: the screen shakes when King Glob lands and when you stomp him, but the score and hearts at the top stay still.

load_level resets boss and shake, and it must do it before the loop that spawns the entities (otherwise it would forget the boss it just spawned):

And the win screen celebrates the right thing now:

Check your work

Run it with the testing line still in and beat King Glob: the win screen says KING GLOB IS DEFEATED!

Then put load_level(1) back in update_title and play the whole game. After the Sky Tower, the throne room plays the boss music and King Glob's health bar appears. He squishes, then hops toward Pip; the screen shakes when he lands; stars circle his head. Stomping him then flashes him red, shakes the screen and shortens the bar. Touching him from the side hurts Pip, unless he's dizzy. At half health he hops faster and brings slimes. The sixth stomp makes him explode and the victory screen appears.

Challenge A ground pound

Make King Glob's landing send a shock wave along the floor: two bullet-like entities that slide left and right from where he lands. Pip has to jump over them.

Hint

Reuse new_bullet(x, y, vx) from lesson 14: one with vx = -2 and one with vx = 2, at floor height.

See what it might look like

Every time King Glob lands, two bullets (new_bullet with vx -2 and 2) slide away from him along the floor: jump over them with Z. This example starts in the throne room.

Challenge Phase three

Add a third phase below 2 hit points: King Glob turns another color (use the palette map from lesson 17) and does two hops in a row before getting dizzy.

See what it might look like

On his last hit point King Glob turns orange (the palette map draws his greens, 6 and 5, as orange 3 and yellow 4) and hops twice in a row before he gets dizzy. This example starts in the throne room; stomp him five times to see it.

Challenge Your own boss

Design a different boss using the same mode-and-timer pattern: a big bat that swoops across the top of the screen and drops bullets, and that can only be hit when it dives low.

See what it might look like

Baron Bat (sprites 326 and 328, 2x2 each) takes King Glob's place: he swoops along the top dropping bullets (new_bullet now takes a vy), then dives at Pip, and only a stomp during the dive hurts him. This example starts in the throne room.

+    x = x - 4, y = y - 8, w = 16,
+    h = 16, vx = 0, vy = 0,
+    hp = BOSS_HP, mode = "wait",
+    timer = 90, flash = 0,
+    update = update_boss,
+    draw = draw_boss
+  })
+end
+
+function update_boss(e)
+  local angry = e.hp <= BOSS_HP // 2
+  e.timer = e.timer - 1
+  e.flash = math.max(0, e.flash - 1)
+  if e.mode == "wait" then
+    if e.timer <= 0 then                       -- jump toward Pip
+      e.mode = "hop"
+      e.vy = angry and -5 or -4.5
+      e.vx =
+        (player.x < e.x and -1 or 1)
+        * (angry and 1.6 or 1.1)
+    end
+  elseif e.mode == "hop" then
+    if move_x(e, e.vx) then   -- bounce off the walls
+      e.vx = -e.vx
+    end
+    e.vy = math.min(e.vy + P.gravity,
+        P.max_fall)
+    if move_y(e, e.vy)
+        and e.vy > 0 then   -- landed: THUD
+      e.vy, e.vx = 0, 0
+      shake = 20
+      play(SND.BUMP)
+      if angry then
+        -- never inside the walls
+        local lo, hi = lvl.x * 8 + 8,
+          (lvl.x + lvl.w) * 8 - 16
+        new_slime(clamp(e.x - 16, lo,
+              hi), e.y + 8)
+        new_slime(clamp(e.x + 24, lo,
+              hi), e.y + 8)
+      end
+      e.mode, e.timer =
+        "dizzy", angry and 60 or 100
+    end
+  elseif e.mode == "dizzy" then
+    if e.timer <= 0 then
+      e.mode, e.timer =
+        "wait", angry and 20 or 50
+    end
+  elseif e.mode == "dying" then
+    if e.timer % 8 == 0 then
+      burst(e.x + math.random(16),
+          e.y + math.random(16), 12,
+          2 + e.timer // 8 % 3)
+      play(SND.EXPLODE)
+    end
+    if e.timer <= 0 then
+      e.dead = true
+      boss = nil
+      set_state("win")
+    end
+    return
+  end
+
+  -- touching King Glob
+  local p = player
+  if overlaps(p, e) then
+    local from_above = p.vy > 0
+      and p.y + p.h - p.vy <= e.y + 4
+    if from_above then
+      p.y = e.y - p.h                          -- on top of him, not inside
+      p.vy, p.jumping = -3.5, false            -- always bounce off his head
+      if e.mode == "dizzy" then
+        hit_boss(e)
+      end
+    elseif e.mode ~= "dizzy" then
+      hurt(e.x + 8)
+    end
+  end
+end
+
+function hit_boss(e)
+  e.hp = e.hp - 1
+  e.flash = 30
+  shake = 10
+  score = score + 500
+  play(SND.BOSS_HIT)
+  burst(e.x + 8, e.y, 12, 4)
+  if e.hp <= 0 then
+    e.mode, e.timer = "dying", 120
+  else
+    e.mode, e.timer = "wait", 40
+  end
+end
+
+function draw_boss(e)
+  local id = SPR_BOSS
+  if e.flash > 0
+      or e.mode == "dying" then
+    id = SPR_BOSS_HURT
+  elseif e.mode == "dizzy"
+      or (e.mode == "wait"
+        and e.timer <= 15) then
+    id = SPR_BOSS_SQUISH                       -- squashed down: dizzy, or about to jump
+  end
+  -- spr(id, x, y, colorkey, scale, flip, rotate, w, h): w, h = 2 draws 2x2 sprites
+  spr(id, e.x - cam.x, e.y - cam.y, 0,
+      1, player.x > e.x and 1 or 0,
+      0, 2, 2)
+  if e.mode == "dizzy" then                    -- stars circling his head
+    for i = 0, 2 do
+      local a = t / 10 + i * 2.1
+      spr(SPR_HUD_STAR,
+          e.x + 4 + math.cos(a) * 9
+          - cam.x, e.y - 9 + math.sin(
+            a) * 3 - cam.y, 0)
+    end
+  end
+end
+
+function draw_boss_bar()
+  if not boss then return end
+  print("KING GLOB", 92, 12, 12)
+  rect(70, 20, 100, 4, 15)
+  rect(70, 20,
+      100 * boss.hp // BOSS_HP, 4, 2)
+end
+
 -- == Power-ups ==
 -- Pip's head hit something solid: open any ?-block above it.

Lesson 20 of 20 · 90 minutes

Polish and ship

Finish the game with a title menu, a saved game to continue, fade-ins, dust, a pause-menu entry and an ending, then test it and publish it as a web game anyone can play.

In this lesson

  • saving with pmem
  • a title menu
  • fading the palette
  • small effects that make a game feel finished
  • the game menu (-- menu: and MENU)
  • playtesting
  • exporting to HTML and publishing on itch.io

Starting point: lesson19.png · Finished: lesson20.png · Play it

Step 1 Polish: what makes a game feel finished

Polish is the many small things that make it feel good: the screen fading in, dust under Pip's feet, a title screen that remembers you, an ending that says thank you.

Step 2 Saving progress with pmem

A player who reached the Sky Tower shouldn't have to start from the meadow every time. TIC-80 gives every cart 256 numbers that are kept when the game is turned off: pmem(slot) reads one, pmem(slot, value) writes it. (In the browser they're kept in the browser's storage, per game.)

New and changed definitions outside the functions (constants, tables, variables): add these to your cart, or replace the old version of the same lines.

Check

Run it (CtrlR): nothing changes yet, but there's no error.

math.max makes sure a save never goes backwards: replaying level 1 doesn't overwrite a save at level 3, and a worse score doesn't replace the best one. The game saves when a new level starts, at game over and at the end; after winning, the saved level goes back to 1, so the next game starts from the beginning:

TIC-80 files a cart's pmem under a fingerprint of the cart's graphics, map and sounds, so changing a single sprite makes the game forget its save. A -- saveid: line in the header gives the save a fixed name instead; add one now: -- saveid: pips-peak.

Check

Run it and lose all your lives. Press Esc until you see the console, and type eval trace(pmem(1)): it shows your score, saved as the best. (Finish the meadow instead, and eval trace(pmem(0)) shows 2: the level you reached.)

Step 3 A title menu

The title screen gets a menu: NEW GAME, and, if there's a saved level, CONTINUE at that level. Up and Down move between them (3 - menu_pos swaps 1 and 2):

The title also has twinkling stars (16 pixels that move slowly and change color), Pip drawn at scale 2 (spr's fifth argument), the best score and the controls. BTN_UP = 0 is one of the new constants above.

CONTINUE only shows once the save says level 2 or later. To try it without playing that far, add this testing line on its own, right below local SAVE_LEVEL, SAVE_BEST = 0, 1:

It pretends you've reached the throne room. You'll take it out at the end of the lesson.

Check

Run it: twinkling stars, a big Pip, your best score, and NEW GAME and CONTINUE (THRONE ROOM). Up and Down move the pointer; Z on CONTINUE starts in the throne room.

Step 4 Fade in

Lesson 4 changed the palette in memory to make night fall. The same trick makes every scene fade in from black: keep a copy of the palette, and for the first 20 frames of a state, write darker versions of it into palette memory.

Check

Run it: nothing changes yet, but there's no error.

k goes from nearly 0 (almost black) to 1 (full color) as fade counts down; every red, green and blue value is multiplied by it. Call save_palette() in BOOT, and start a fade there too, for the title screen:

(The testing line stays where it is: it's outside BOOT.)

Start the fade in set_state as well (but not for the dead and level-clear states, which should stay on screen as they are):

and call apply_fade() at the very end of TIC. TIC-80 reads the palette when it shows the frame, so changing it after drawing still colors the whole frame.

Check

Run it: the title fades in from black, and so does the level when you start a game.

Step 5 Dust

Small puffs of gray particles when Pip runs and when it lands hard:

t % 8 == 0 makes a puff every 8 frames, behind Pip's feet (- dir * 3). And a puff on hard landings:

Check

Run it and hold Right: little gray puffs behind Pip's feet. Jump off something high: a puff when it lands.

Step 6 The game menu

In a running TIC-80 game, Esc opens a menu (resume, reset, close…). A cart can add its own entries with a -- menu: line in its header, next to -- title: and -- author::

Each word is an entry. They appear under GAME MENU, and choosing one calls the cart's MENU function with the entry's number, starting from 0:

RESTART costs a life (otherwise it would be a free escape from any danger); TITLE saves and goes back to the title screen.

Once the cart has a -- menu: line, the game keeps Esc and the F keys while it runs, even when you start it with CtrlR: Esc opens the menu instead of going back to the editor. To get back to the editor, choose CLOSE GAME in that menu.

Check

Run it, start a game and press Esc: GAME MENU has RESTART and TITLE. RESTART costs a life; TITLE goes back to the title screen. On the title screen they do nothing.

Step 7 The ending

The win screen shows the score and thanks the player:

Put your own name in the cart's header (-- author:), with a one-line description of the game in -- desc::

Check

Run it, choose CONTINUE (THRONE ROOM) and beat King Glob: the new ending, with your score and "thanks for playing!".

Now take the testing line pmem(0, 4) out. Winning set the save back to level 1, so the next game starts from the meadow.

Step 8 Playtest

Before you publish, play the whole game, start to finish, and then ask someone else to play it without your help. Watch, don't explain: everywhere they get stuck is something to fix. Check:

  • Every level can be finished, and the gems can be reached (some are meant to be tricky, none impossible).
  • Losing all lives, then CONTINUE, puts you back at the saved level with full lives.
  • The game menu entries work, during play and on the title screen (where they do nothing).
  • Sounds and music: nothing is too loud, nothing cuts off the music.
  • Nothing happens that depends on how fast the computer is: everything in the game counts frames, not time().
  • The game is fair: the first time a new danger appears, there's room to see it before it hurts.

TIC-80's trace() prints values to the console.

Step 9 Export for the web

TIC-80 can turn a cart into a web page that runs in any browser, with no install. In the console:

export html downloads the web player from tic80.com (you need an internet connection), puts your cart in it and saves pips-peak.zip in your TIC-80 folder (type folder to open it). The zip holds an index.html, the player and your cart.

The index.html won't run if you double-click it: browsers don't allow it from a file. It needs a web server: the next step puts it on itch.io.

Step 10 Publish on itch.io

itch.io hosts web games for free.

  1. Make an account, then Upload new project.
  2. Set Kind of project to HTML.
  3. Upload pips-peak.zip and tick This file will be played in the browser.
  4. Set the viewport to 960 x 544 (four times TIC-80's 240 x 136) and tick Fullscreen button.
  5. Add a cover image (F8 in TIC-80 saves a screenshot; F9 starts and stops recording a GIF), a description, and the controls.
  6. Save, look at the page, and when you're happy, set it to Public.

Check your work

The title screen fades in, plays its music and shows NEW GAME (and CONTINUE once you've reached a later level). Running kicks up dust. Esc → GAME MENU shows RESTART and TITLE. Beating King Glob shows the thank-you screen and saves the best score. The exported zip runs in a browser and on itch.io.

Step 11 What next?

You've built a whole platformer: physics, a camera, tiles and levels, collectibles, enemies, power-ups, sound, music, a boss and a finished, published game.

Challenge Make it yours

Make a fifth level with your own idea: a new tile with a new flag (wind? water? a tile that only exists every other second?), a new enemy built from the entity pieces, and a new track. Add it to LEVELS before the throne room.

Challenge A level timer

Show a timer in the HUD, and save the best time for each level in pmem (slots 2-5). Show the best times on the title screen.

See what it might look like

The HUD shows the level's time (level_t, as minutes, seconds and tenths); finishing a level keeps its time in pmem slot 2-5 if it's the best, and the title screen lists the best times.

Challenge A second character

Draw a second character with different tuning (P): faster but jumping lower, or slower with a double jump of its own. Let the player pick one on the title screen. (Careful with "lower": the levels have steps three tiles high, 24 pixels, so jump_speed can't be weaker than about -3.75.)

See what it might look like

Kit the fox (sprites 368-377, each one 112 after the Pip sprite with the same pose) runs faster but jumps lower: a copy of P with three changes. Press Left or Right on the title screen to pick Kit or Pip, then Z.

Challenge Share it

Publish your game, and play other people's TIC-80 games on tic80.com/play. Reading other carts' code (in TIC-80, surf browses them) is one of the best ways to learn new tricks.

Helpful tip

Loading a lesson cart

Open a lesson's finished cart in TIC-80, or take just one part of it.

A PNG cart

Each lesson has its finished cart at the top of the page. It is a PNG cart: a picture of the game with the whole cart hidden inside it. Your computer shows it as a picture, and TIC-80 loads the game from it.

To load it, drag the file onto the TIC-80 window. Or put it in TIC-80's folder (type folder in the console to open it) and type:

Then save it under your own name, so your work doesn't change the lesson's file:

Anything that saves the picture again throws the cart away: a paint program, a chat app, a photo site. Download it and load it straight into TIC-80.

Just one part

You can take one part of a lesson cart and keep the rest of yours. Load your own cart first, then type the part after the file name:

The part can be code, tiles, sprites, map, flags, sfx, music or palette. It replaces that part of your cart, so save afterwards.

Helpful tip

Saving your carts

Where TIC-80 keeps your carts, and how not to lose one.

Save often

Type save pips-peak in the console once. After that, CtrlS saves the cart under that name from anywhere in TIC-80.

Where your carts are

Type folder in the console. TIC-80 opens the folder it keeps your carts in. Everything you save goes there. dir lists the files and cd changes folder, inside TIC-80.

If you use TIC-80 in a web browser, your carts are kept inside that browser. Use the same browser on the same computer each time.

Keep a copy

Before a big change, save a copy under another name:

Then load pips-peak to go back to your cart. If the change goes wrong, load pips-peak-backup brings the old one back.

Helpful tip

Keys and the console

The keys you use all the time, and the console commands for carts.

Keys

KeyDoes
EscLeave the game; switch between the console and the editors
F1 … F5Code, sprite, map, sound and music editors
CtrlRRun the game
CtrlSSave the cart
Arrows, ZMove and jump in the game

Console commands

CommandDoes
new luaStart a new cart that uses Lua
save pips-peakSave the cart
load pips-peakLoad a cart
runRun the game
dir, cdList the files in the current folder, change folder
folderOpen the folder TIC-80 keeps your carts in
help commandsList every command
clsClear the console

Helpful tip

When something breaks

What to do when your game shows an error or doesn't do what the lesson says.

Read the error

When the code has a mistake, TIC-80 stops the game and shows an error in the console. It says the line number. Press F1 and look at that line, and the one above it. The usual causes:

  • a missing end, or one too many;
  • a typo in a name: Lua cares about capital letters, so Cls is not cls;
  • a name you haven't made yet, or made in a later step.

Compare with the lesson

At the bottom of every lesson you can open the whole cart's code after that lesson, and every change since the lesson before. Find the function that misbehaves and compare it with yours, line by line.

Start from the lesson's cart

If you can't find it, load the lesson's finished cart (Loading a lesson cart) and carry on from there. Keep your own cart under its name, so you can come back to it.

Bonus lesson · 40 minutes

Pixel art in 8x8

How the pictures in Pip's Peak were drawn, and how to draw your own: the shape first, a few colors, light from one side, clean lines, tiles that join up, and frames that move.

In this lesson

  • start with the shape
  • pick a few colors from the palette
  • light from one side
  • clean lines and lone pixels
  • tiles that join up
  • animation frames
  • the whole collection, drawn step by step

Not needed for the game: take it any time after lesson 2.

Step 1 64 pixels

A sprite in TIC-80 is 8 x 8 pixels: 64 in all. That's tiny, so every pixel counts. One pixel can be an eye, a shine, a mouth. It's also why 8 x 8 is a great way to learn pixel art: you can try an idea in a minute, and CtrlZ takes it back in a second.

You don't need this lesson for the game. At the bottom is the whole collection: every picture in Pip's Peak, each with an animation of it being drawn in TIC-80's sprite editor.

Step 2 Start with the shape

Before any detail, draw the silhouette: the shape of the thing, all in one color. If you can tell what it is from the shape alone, you'll recognize it in the game too, where it is small and moving.

Squint at a sprite, or step back from the screen: what's left is the shape. A slime is a blob, a coin is a circle, Pip is a sprout with a leaf and two feet.

A drawing that starts from nothing goes like this: the outline in the main color, the fill tool for the inside, then the details on top. Thin things, like the fence, are just lines; a block gets its frame drawn round the edge first.

Step 3 A few colors, picked on purpose

TIC-80 has 16 colors, and most sprites here use three or four. Fewer colors make a sprite cleaner, and they make your game look like one world.

The palette is built in ramps: colors that go from dark to light. To shade something, use the darker color next to it in its ramp; to light it, the lighter one.

Step 4 Light from one side

Pick where the light comes from (top left is the usual choice) and stick to it: the side facing the light gets the lighter color, the other side the darker one. A common mistake is pillow shading: dark all around the edge, light in the middle, as if the light came from the front. It looks puffy and flat.

Look at the coin above: the shine is on the left, the orange shading on the right, and every coin, gem and heart in the game follows the same light.

Step 5 Clean lines, and pixels that belong

A slanted line looks smooth when its steps are even: 2, 2, 2 or 1, 1, 1. Uneven steps (1, then 3, then 1) look like a mistake, and the eye catches them.

Every pixel should belong to something. A lone pixel that isn't part of a shape looks like dirt on the screen, unless it's on purpose: Pip's eye is one pixel, and so are the specks in the dirt tile. If you can't say what a pixel is for, try the sprite without it.

Step 6 Tiles that join up

A ground tile is drawn once and placed hundreds of times, side by side. So its left edge must fit its own right edge, and its bottom must fit the tile under it. Draw one end first, then make the middle and the other end from copies, changing only the edges that differ.

The grass was drawn left to right: tile 1 first, then tile 2 from a copy of it (CtrlC, click the next slot, CtrlV), changing only what differs. The right end, tile 3, is the left end's mirror image: another copy of tile 1, flipped with FLIP HORZ, and a few specks moved.

To test a tile, paint a row of it in the map editor (or the Map Lab of lesson 6): a seam shows straight away.

Step 7 Frames that move

An animation is a few pictures shown one after another, and good frames change very little: in Pip's run, the body moves one pixel and the feet swap. The coin spins by getting thinner and wider again.

So each frame starts as a copy of one before it. When a whole part moves, the select tool and the arrows round the canvas nudge it a pixel without redrawing it:

When Pip lands from a jump, the game shows a squashed Pip for a moment: wider and lower, so it looks soft. The same trick works for anything that bounces.

Step 8 Bigger than 8 x 8

King Glob is 16 x 16: four sprites in a square (320, 321, 336 and 337). Drawing a quarter at a time would make the seams hard to match, so set CANVAS ZOOM (the slider at the top right of the sprite editor) to its second stop: the canvas then holds all four, and you draw the whole king at once. spr(320, x, y, 0, 1, 0, 0, 2, 2) draws the four together.

Step 9 Your turn

Open the finished game's cart in the Sprite Lab below (or your own cart in TIC-80) and draw in an empty slot:

  1. A key. The shape first in yellow, the shadow side in orange, one white pixel of shine.
  2. A mushroom. A red cap with white spots and a pale stem. Then make a "bad" mushroom by changing only its colors.
  3. A blink. Copy Pip (256) into an empty slot and close its eye: two frames make a blink.
  4. A new ground tile, like sand or snow, with a top edge and a middle, that joins up with itself. Paint a row of it on the map to check.

The lab plays the animations of the game's code while you draw, and ▶ Try it in the game shows your changes in the game.

Step 10 The collection

Every picture in Pip's Peak, by kind. Click one to watch it being drawn in TIC-80's sprite editor, and to see its pixel rows (one digit per pixel: the color number, 0 for empty). Draw along, or use it as a start for your own.
